title: Dan Campbell remembers 9/11 as Detroit Lions to honor first responders
summary: Prior to kickoff in the Detroit Lions’ 2026 season opener at Ford Field, the team will honor about 30 local Detroit first responders, 16 of whom personally took time out of their lives to travel to New York 25 years ago to lend a helping hand in the aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. When […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 23: A giant American Flag is displayed on the field during the playing of the National Anthem before the start of a traditional Thanksgiving Day NFL football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions on November 23, 2023 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Prior to kickoff in the Detroit Lions’ 2026 season opener at Ford Field, the team will honor about 30 local Detroit first responders, 16 of whom personally took time out of their lives to travel to New York 25 years ago to lend a helping hand in the aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. When Lions coach Dan Campbell stepped to his press conference on Friday, the 25th anniversary of 9/11, he was sporting a Detroit Fire Department hat as a nod to their service. Campbell has a personal connection to the 9/11 aftermath. At the time, Campbell was in just his third year of the NFL, all as a member of the New York Giants. Campbell was among several members of the Giants and Jets who traveled to Ground Zero to offer any sort of help they could. “It’s something you never forget, being up there. You get the worst of humanity, and you get the best all in a matter of minutes,” Campbell said. “One of the most inspiring things that you could ever witness, be around, is in the middle of a tragedy—especially in New York, where people, man, they’re in a hurry. It’s about getting to one spot to another, and you’ve got places to go, things to do, and that happens. And man, everybody just pitches in to help. They just want to help and do whatever it takes.” Coach Campbell reflects on his memories from Sept. 11, 2001 pic.twitter.com/X9NKwp82do — Detroit Lions (@Lions) September 11, 2026 At the time, Campbell remembers feeling helpless to provide any true physical help. But he has since realized the impact his presence had on the people who were sacrificing everything to make a difference. “I didn’t understand that. We just wanted to help. We could do nothing, compared to what they were doing,” Campbell said of the first responders on scene. “Those guys didn’t sleep. Those first responders, man, there was no sleep, there were no showers, there was no food, there was no… “And the fact that we were able to go when we go, just to help where we could—we were just trying to, ‘What can we grab? What can we do?’ And they just wanted us—us being there meant a lot to them, and I just remember thinking how humbling that was. Like, ‘We’re not doing anything.’ But it did; I think it gave them a little pep, and it’s a reminder that you may not think it can be powerful, but just your presence and being around there and letting them know you’re thinking about them and you just want to help them help others. It goes a long way.” That’s why it was important for Campbell to honor not just the 16 first responders that traveled hundreds of miles that week, but all first responders that sacrifice so much for the health and safety of others. “It’s significant, man. It’s unselfishness, and it’s just wanting to help. All you have is yourself, and you’re going to give up your time,” Campbell said. “I mean, you dig through that rubble. It’s not like that was some safe place to go out there and do what you do. So yeah, it means a lot. You start talking about these first responders, fire department, police department, certainly everybody that deals with healthcare at that time, just trying to do what they can.”

title: Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell offers big update on LG competition
summary: At the beginning of the week, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell dropped an interesting update that the left guard position was still up for grabs in the lead up to the team’s season opener against the New Orleans Saints. Incumbent Christian Mahogany and free agent addition Ben Bartch were to split reps in practice all […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - OCTOBER 12: Christian Mahogany #73 of the Detroit Lions runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on October 12, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images At the beginning of the week, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell dropped an interesting update that the left guard position was still up for grabs in the lead up to the team’s season opener against the New Orleans Saints. Incumbent Christian Mahogany and free agent addition Ben Bartch were to split reps in practice all week, and Campbell even said he’d consider rotating the two in the game if a leader hadn’t emerged in the competition. But on Friday, Campbell gave a little clarity on the situation, suggesting that Mahogany will start on Sunday. “I don’t know. It’s a good question. I’m still thinking about that. There’s probably a good chance Mahogany starts,” Campbell said. Now, of course, who starts the game and who finishes it could very different. Campbell’s comments are vague enough to suggest that the guard rotation could continue and/or Mahogany could be on a short leash. He could even change his mind before Sunday. Campbell did note that both players have played well in the two practices thus far this week. “I thought both of those guys did a really good job in practice,” Campbell said. That’s as close to an answer as we’re going to get from Campbell until Sunday, and this is a competition that could very well extend beyond Week 1, depending on what happens on the field against the Saints. But for a team that was hoping to get their starting five offensive linemen in place by early training camp, I wouldn’t expect Campbell to drag his feet on this competition much longer.

title: The Honolulu Blueprint: 4 predictions for a Lions victory over the Saints in Week 1
summary: The Detroit Lions and New Orleans Saints will square off in a Week 1 matchup at Ford Field, kicking off the first regular-season game of the 2026 season for each team. “This opponent, it’s a hungry opponent,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said earlier in the week. “It’s a new turnover from what I remember when […]
full_text: Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs (0) celebrates first down against Chicago Bears during the second half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 14, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions and New Orleans Saints will square off in a Week 1 matchup at Ford Field, kicking off the first regular-season game of the 2026 season for each team. “This opponent, it’s a hungry opponent,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said earlier in the week. “It’s a new turnover from what I remember when I was there. There are a few holdovers, but most of this, it’s a new roster. And there’s a lot of young, hungry players, talented players. You could see their progression as the season went on last year towards the end of the year… this will be a good opponent, but we’ve got them in our house, and we’ll be ready to go.” Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict what the Lions will do to earn a victory over the Saints in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint. Saints base schemes For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, make sure you check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 1 preview: Breaking down Saints’ offensive and defensive schemes. Prediction 1: Offense dinks-and-dunks, winning with accuracy and YAC As I talked about in my breakdown of the Saints’ defensive scheme, New Orleans runs a base 3-4 front with a modified version of Vic Fangio’s zone-match coverage scheme on the back end—which has become very popular in recent years. Essentially, the Saints spend a lot of time in Cover-3 (nearly half their defensive snaps in 2025) with multiple linebackers who live in the intermediate range, allowing them to drop into coverage and/or stay close to the line to defend the run. This approach by the Saints keeps bodies up front to stop the run, jams up passing lanes, and protects against the deep ball. To counter this approach, the Lions will need to be patient, be deliberate with their decisions, and take what’s available to them. Fortunately, for Detroit, they have the offensive weapons to put pressure on the Saints’ scheme. With elite weapons in the slot—namely Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta—and a quarterback who is best known for his accuracy, Jared Goff will likely spend most of this game looking to get the ball in his playmakers’ hands and letting them win with yards after the catch (YAC). While this approach from the Lions will require Goff to be consistently accurate and make smart decisions, that’s right in his wheelhouse. Prediction 2: Creative play calling with Jahmyr Gibbs leads to big numbers Sunday will mark Jahmyr Gibbs’ first game as a true “bell cow” back, as the Lions plan to give him the majority of offensive snaps at running back moving forward. The last time Gibbs was the sole primary option at running back was in 2024, when David Montgomery missed time with an MCL injury. In those three games, Gibbs averaged: 21.3 rushing attempts per game 121.7 rushing yards 1.7 touchdowns 3.7 receptions 41 receiving yards Those numbers are terrific, and there are reasons to believe Gibbs could match or exceed that output this season. One of the things that make Gibbs such a dynamic offensive weapon is that he can attack defenses in a variety of ways, and offensive coordinator Drew Petzing has prioritized finding creative ways to get Gibbs the football. Against a Saints front that finished the 2025 season eighth in DVOA vs. the run, Gibbs will be challenged on runs. And while the Lions will certainly try to establish the run as part of their identity, creative play calling by Petzing—getting Gibbs in space via screens, Wheel and Texas routes, etc.—should be the key to breaking through the Saints’ defense. As we saw in those previous “bell cow” games from Gibbs, 25 touches should be expected for the superstar back, and if Petzing shows some of the things we saw in camp, Gibbs will have a chance to put up big numbers. Prediction 3: A lot of “Base” formations vs Saints The Saints finished 27th in passing offense in 2025 , and while starting quarterback Tyler Shough certainly helped improve the unit, they enter the season in the bottom half of most rankings. While the Saints invested in offensive skill players this offseason, they’re dealing with injuries (first-round pick Jordan Tyson is on IR and RB Alvin Kamara is working through an MCL injury) and are still a work in progress. Like the Lions (prior to elevating Tom Kennedy), the Saints are only rostering four wide receivers. Unlike the Lions, most of the Saints’ talent at wide receiver is unproven. Superstar Chris Olave headlines the group, and DeVaughn Vele has shown to be a solid WR2, but behind them, they’re rolling with two Day 3 rookies. Now, the Saints do have a solid tight end in Juwan Johnson, which gives them a third pass-catching option, but New Orleans will likely need to rely heavily on their running backs. With top free-agent acquisition running back Travis Etienne expected to start and be heavily involved in the Saints’ offensive attack, look for the Lions to counter with “base” defense to fill rushing gaps and challenge the Saints to go to the air. Furthermore, as pointed out by Anthony Balaj in his key player matchup preview , “the Saints and Shough ranked 30th in the NFL in play-action rate at just 18.6% in 2025, per NFL NextGen Stats ,” which should further allow the Lions to stay in base. With no real threat of disguise from the offense, the Lions can confidently play off their keys with their base personnel, thus allowing them to be in better positions more consistently. This approach would also allow the Lions to unleash some of the new “juice” they acquired in the offseason. Prediction 4: Offseason “Juice” leads to increased pressures and sacks The Saints quarterback room is still very young, and while there are a lot of encouraging signs for Shough’s development, one area he struggled with last season was sacks. In 2025, the Saints surrendered 49 sacks (2.88 per game), with Shough giving up 31 in his nine starts (averaging over three sacks per game). The story was similar with pressures; as a whole team, they surrendered 227 (13.4 per game), with Shough succumbing to 119 (13.22 per game). In addition to relying on Shough’s experience to help them improve in this area, the Saints also made a point to address their offensive line this offseason and made a strong move by signing LG David Edwards. On paper, the Saints certainly upgraded their offensive line, but they’ll be tested early with the Lions’ new defensive front. “There’s an emphasis (on adding pass-rushing talent this offseason); we wanted to add more juice and more ability to get after the quarterback,” general manager Brad Holmes said earlier this month. Last season, the Lions’ pass-rushing statistics were respectable. They finished the season with 49 sacks (fourth most in the NFL) and 235 pressures (seventh), but they struggled immensely in one area: Time to pressure. On average, the Lions took 2.86 seconds to generate pressure (30th in the NFL), and they made a strong offseason effort to improve in this area. The first and most obvious way the Lions improved in this area was player talent. They signed DJ Wommum and drafted Derrick Moore (in the second round) to reinvigorate their rush end position, while also getting more athletic inside by expanding Mekhi Wingo’s role and drafting Skyler Gill-Howard. Alim McNeill’s return to full health and Tyleik Williams’s second-year development also helped boost the Lions in this area. The second and less obvious way the Lions improved their pass rush was in their schematic approach. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard insists that the Lions aren’t doing anything new up front, but the difference on the field has been noticeable. This could simply be a matter of getting the “right” guys into the scheme, but I believe Sheppard is leaning more into the athleticism of his front than in the past, which allows him to use more stunts, cross-face approaches, and…

title: Detroit Lions vs. New Orleans Saints preview, prediction: On Paper
summary: Welcome back to another season of On Paper, my statistical-heavy Detroit Lions preview that attempts to be as objective as possible. For those new to On Paper, a brief explanation. At the heart of On Paper are eight charts that detail each team’s primary units (pass offense, run offense, pass defense, run defense). Those charts […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - DECEMBER 03: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions throws a pass in the first quarter against the New Orleans Saints at the Caesars Superdome on December 03, 2023 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to another season of On Paper, my statistical-heavy Detroit Lions preview that attempts to be as objective as possible. For those new to On Paper, a brief explanation. At the heart of On Paper are eight charts that detail each team’s primary units (pass offense, run offense, pass defense, run defense). Those charts are filled with weekly performances that compare it to the opponent’s average. This provides proper context to show that holding the Lions passing offense to 120 yards is much different than holding the Jets to that yardage. Cells that are green indicate a better than average performance, yellow is within 5% of averages, and red means you stunk that week. Then we compare the units that face off. If there’s one thing about NFL previews that enrages me, it’s when analysts compare units (ie: who has the better offense, defense, QB?). That doesn’t matter. The quarterbacks don’t ever share the field. Instead, it matters how the Lions pass offense matches with the opponent’s pass defense. So after throwing a bunch of stats at you, I provide a key matchup and my overall thoughts on who has the advantage in each matchup—which is graded on a 1-5 scale based on how big the advantage is, how important I believe that matchup is to the overall outcome, and just my overall confidence. This is the only part that is a bit subjective. At the end, I add up all the advantages, see who has the edge, and provide a final score prediction. In the comments, be sure to give your score prediction. The closest to the actual score will get a shout out in next week’s On Paper . Now, let’s get to it. Lions pass offense (6th in DVOA in 2025) vs. Saints pass defense (19th) Despite a running game that fell apart, significant issues on the offensive line, and an offensive coordinator that just didn’t fit, Jared Goff and the Lions passing offense remained pretty efficient all season. The 2025 season will always be a great counter-example to those who claim Goff needs everything to be perfect around him to be successful. In 2025, the Lions and Goff finished: 4th in yards per attempt (7.4) 3rd in passer rating (103.6) 7th in dropback EPA (0.167) 9th in dropback success rate (48.5%) By nearly every metric, this was a top-10 passing offense. So what has changed this year? Well, in terms of weapons, nothing is really all that different. Sam LaPorta is healthier, Isaac TeSlaa is a year older, and that’s about it. But the offensive line has been completely revamped. Penei Sewell went from right to left tackle. Rookie Blake Miller takes his spot on the right. Cade Mays Juice Scruggs takes over at center for Graham Glasgow. And Ben Bartch and Christian Mahogany are still battling for the left guard position. Second-year right guard Tate Ratledge? You just stay there and keep being you. Pass protection was an issue last year. Despite Goff being one of the quickest quarterbacks in time-to-throw (fifth), he also faced the 14th-highest pressure rate, and took a career-high 38 sacks (eighth among all NFL quarterbacks). The Lions also ranked 31st in ESPN’s pass block win rate and 24th in PFF pass blocking grade. Are the Lions decidedly better on the offensive line in 2026? It’s impossible to know right now, but I’m not entirely optimistic it will look better to start the year given just how many moving parts there are. So some protection issues should be expected early, but Goff should still be able to orchestrate at a top-10 level of efficiency. The Saints’ pass defense wasn’t good last year, but as you can see from the chart, it got significantly better as the season went on. Part of that is due to playing ONLY terrible passing offenses in their final eight games, but it’s reasonable to think they also improved as a unit down the stretch. If you didn’t pay attention to the quality of their opponents, the difference between the first and second half of the season would be incredibly stark: Weeks 1-9 29th in passer rating allowed (107.2) 26th in dropback EPA 27th in dropback success rate Week 10-18 7th in passer rating allowed (74.7) 5th in dropback EPA 1st in dropback success rate Those are drastic swings and shouldn’t be ignored completely. It’s very normal for a team to start figuring things out in Year 1 of a new coaching staff toward the end of the season. But… also… just look at those offenses. They didn’t face a single team who averaged a passer rating above 90 in their final eight games. That makes trying to predict how 2026 will go difficult. The Saints didn’t make a ton of changes on defense this offseason. They lost linebacker Demario Davis but replaced him with a far younger Kaden Ellis. They also bolstered the interior of their defensive line with second-round pick Christen Miller… but they lost Brian Bresee to a season-ending injury and Cam Jordan won’t play this week. Last year, the Saints were pretty inconsistent as a pass rushing team. They ranked 24th in pressure rate (31.9%), 23rd in PFF pass rushing grade (66.6), and 22nd in ESPN pass rush win rate (35%), but they still produced the 10th-most sacks. Coverage was a different story. Kool-Aid McKinstry had a bit of a breakout year (17 passes defended, 3 INTs), and the Saints sport a trusted safety duo in Justin Reid (66.7 PFF grade last year) and Julian Blackmon (82.4). Player to watch: Chase Young vs. Blake Miller. Right, I forgot about Young. Despite playing just 12 games, he produced 49 pressures and 10.0 sacks. Last year, he almost played exclusively opposite the left tackle (529 snaps there vs. just 13 on the right), but I wouldn’t be surprised to see New Orleans change up strategy when the options are Penei Sewell or a rookie in his first NFL game. Advantage: Lions +1. I’m probably not going to move far from +1s early in the season with very little relevant data to go off of. However, I can feel pretty confident in Detroit here because they’ve been doing it longer and more consistently, and I’m still not sure who the Saints are just because they played a bunch of terrible offenses to finish 2025. Lions run offense (10th) vs. Saints run defense (8th) After some inconsistent—but occasionally great—performances early in the season, Detroit’s run offense absolutely collapsed down the stretch, and it was a big part of their downfall—losing four of their last six games. The season-long stats are not encouraging. Detroit ranked just: 9th in yards per carry (4.6) 23rd in rush EPA (-0.037) 16th in rushing success rate (41.0%) The only thing that kept Detroit’s stats even mildly afloat were the explosive runs from Jahmyr Gibbs. He ranked ninth in 10+ yard rushes (27), third in 20+ yard rushes (10), and t-second in 30+ yard rushes (six). The Lions offensive line ranked 13th in PFF run grade, 20th in run block win rate, and 20th in adjusted line yards. There is hope the offensive line changes and a switch to a more innovative offensive coordinator will help out the run game this year, but that remains a theory, not a fact. The Saints gave up a lot of rushing yardage last year (2050, 14th most), but that was largely a result of always trailing in games and facing the third most rushing attempts in the league. On a per-play, basis, they were actually quite sound. In 2025, they ranked: Eighth in yards per carry allowed (4.0) 2nd in rush EPA (-0.136) 9th in rush success rate (39.0%) That’s the bad news for Detroit. The good news? Two of the Saints best run defenders from last year will not be playing in this game. Demario Davis—their leader and best linebacker who posted an 89.3 run defense grade—left in free agency. And veteran defensive lineman (82.1 grade) Cam Jordan is out with an injury. Kaden Ellis, the linebacker they added this offseason, doesn’t…
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Lions vs. Saints preview: 3 key player matchups
summary: The Detroit Lions and the New Orleans Saints will open their 2026 campaigns at Ford Field, both hungry to put their respective fourth-place division finishes in the rearview mirror. Despite each sharing last-place finishes in 2025, that is about the only thing the Lions and Saints have in common headed into the new season. New […]
full_text: The Detroit Lions and the New Orleans Saints will open their 2026 campaigns at Ford Field, both hungry to put their respective fourth-place division finishes in the rearview mirror. Despite each sharing last-place finishes in 2025, that is about the only thing the Lions and Saints have in common headed into the new season. New Orleans is in year two of Kellen Moore’s tenure as head coach, and after a promising rookie season, Tyler Shough opens the season as the starting quarterback. At the top of the roster, wide receiver Chris Olave is likely the only All-Pro who will be active on gameday while still in a starting role. All-Pro running back Alvin Kamara has been recovering from an MCL sprain through training camp ( but could play ) while the Saints have added running back Travis Etienne to the room this offseason. Further, All-Pro defensive end Cam Jordan has been ruled out for the game with a hamstring injury. In contrast, the Lions will field young, All-Pro talents on both sides of the ball with Jack Campbell, Aidan Hutchinson, Amon-Ra St. Brown, and Penei Sewell. Beyond that, Jared Goff is entering his sixth season as the Lions’ quarterback, while Jahmyr Gibbs is the betting favorite for Offensive Player of the Year and was likely drafted as the first pick in most fantasy football drafts across the country. Why am I so focused on the blue-chip talent on each roster? Well, it is because identifying winning matchups and exploiting them is the center of Dan Campbell’s philosophy: “Here’s my philosophy on offense, and defense for that matter: We’re going to run a system that puts our best on your worst. That’s what we’re going to do because that’s what we did in New Orleans. We’re going to find a way to put our guys in one-one-one matchups, whether it’s run or pass. If you’re telling me that our left tackle is better than their right end, and we can run outside zone all day – we’re going to run outside zone, as long as we cut off the back side. Why not? If we can exploit a weakness, we’re going to do it.” With the apparent advantage the Lions have in elite talent at each level of the field on both sides of the ball, there should be plenty of areas where the coaching staff can dictate winning matchups. Let’s take a look at three of them. Jack Campbell vs. Tyler Shough It’s officially Captain Jack season. Jack Campbell enters his first year as a captain and the green-dot linebacker with complete ownership of the defense, facing a young passer in Shough. Campbell enters the year with this defense being his now. And it’s not just talk. Second-year defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard let him call the defense from the field for a full practice during training camp. Captain Jack Campbell. pic.twitter.com/oGMI1GMb36 — Detroit Lions (@Lions) September 8, 2026 With all due respect to the ascending quarterback, Shough will simply be in a very difficult environment to succeed on Sunday. In his favor, Shough will play behind what appears to be a strong offensive line on paper. From left to right, the line includes 2025 first-round pick Kelvin Banks Jr., newly acquired left guard David Edwards, Erik McCoy at center, right guard Cesar Ruiz, and 2024 first-round pick Taliese Fuaga at right tackle. Conventional wisdom would suggest that head coach Kellen Moore will try to support his young quarterback by leaning heavily on the run game behind this offensive line. But that creates an interesting opportunity for Campbell to show off his command of the defense. As the quarterback of the defense, Campbell will be responsible for communicating and adapting Kelvin Sheppard’s evolving disguise-oriented scheme . The Saints and Shough ranked 30th in the NFL in play action rate at just 18.6% in 2025, per NFL NextGen Stats . If New Orleans wants to establish the run but not put Detroit’s box defenders in conflict through play action, then Campbell’s job on gameday is one layer less complicated. The less Campbell is forced to be reactive, the more he can lead the Lions defense. D.J. Reed vs. Chris Olave While the Lions have plenty of blue-chip talent, the one area of the team that is lacking elite, proven talent is the secondary. Expect the Saints to try to use their best matchup piece, Chris Olave, to their advantage. But it might not be that simple. Just as only four wide receivers made the Lions’ initial 53-man roster, the Saints also kept only four on the active roster: Olave, Devaughn Vele, and rookies Bryce Lance and Barion Brown. Missing from this list is 2026 first-round pick Jordyn Tyson. As a result, the key matchup to watch is Lions cornerback D.J. Reed against Olave. The question of whether Reed can bounce back after his first season in Detroit was hampered by a significant hamstring injury will be critically telling about the team’s ultimate ceiling. Week 1 will be an excellent first test. Olave finished the 2025 season with a 27.9 percent target share for the Saints, which ranked seventh among wide receivers who had at least 100 targets on the year, per NFL NextGen Stats . Kelvin Sheppard will have a few options to slow down the Saints offense. Without a true stable of experienced wide receivers available for New Orleans, Sheppard will have the luxury of devoting more resources to stop the run, put pressure on the passer, or mix double coverage looks toward Olave. But the best-case scenario is if Reed can match up with Olave stride for stride. If Reed can limit the All-Pro receiver to a modest season opener, the options for Sheppard become variable and unpredictable. That makes Reed’s assignment more than just an individual matchup, but an opportunity to give Sheppard more freedom for the rest of the defense. Detroit interior OL vs. New Orleans interior DL One of the biggest questions of training camp in Detroit has been how the interior offensive line would look after the position battle at left guard between Christian Mahogany and Ben Bartch, along with newly acquired center Cade Mays. Well, the injury to Mays means Juice Scruggs is in line to be the starting center likely until the Week 6 bye, and Bartch’s battle through his own injuries has given the edge to the guard spot to Mahogany (for now) . Right guard, however, is a different story. Second-year, second-round pick Tate Ratledge is poised to break out after a strong finish to 2025 that has carried over into a strong 2026 training camp. Across the line, the Lions’ interior three will face a Saints group that is missing its best defensive tackle. Bryan Breese suffered a season-ending ACL injury early in camp , leaving New Orleans vulnerable. To fill the void, the Saints will show a rotation of veterans Davon Godchaux, Nathan Shepherd, John Ridgeway, and rookie second-round pick Christen Miller. This creates an opportunity for Detroit. Will the competition and depth in the Lions offensive line room prove themselves against a favorable matchup? Or will the offensive line start off on a poor note, inviting the same criticisms that followed the 2025 opener at Lambeau Field? The performance of Mahogany ( and/or Bartch ), Scruggs, and Ratledge will be under the magnifying glass of many Lions fans. Three key matchups. Three opportunities. Jack Campbell has an opportunity to make life difficult for a young quarterback. D.J. Reed has a chance to neutralize the Saints’ most prolific threat. And the Lions’ interior offensive line has a runway to establish itself against a New Orleans front missing one of its best players. It’s not a light; it’s a freight train. It’s about to be fun.

title: Packers release WR Bo Melton, intend to retain him on practice squad
summary: Just over 48 hours ahead of their season opener, the Green Bay Packers have made a mildly shocking roster move. According to Adam Schefter of ESPN, the Packers are releasing wide receiver Bo Melton on Friday. Melton has been a mainstay of the Packers’ special teams units for the past two-plus years and has remained […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-NOVEMBER 27: Green Bay Packers cornerback Bo Melton #16 during the first half of an NFL football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Thursday, November 27, 2025 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Just over 48 hours ahead of their season opener, the Green Bay Packers have made a mildly shocking roster move. According to Adam Schefter of ESPN, the Packers are releasing wide receiver Bo Melton on Friday. Melton has been a mainstay of the Packers’ special teams units for the past two-plus years and has remained a valuable depth piece in the wide receiver room, even despite being his supposed position switch to cornerback for the 2025 season. As one of the team’s primary punt gunners and kickoff coverage players, Melton logged over 300 special teams snaps across the last two seasons, and the team’s coverage units visibly suffered late in 2025 when he missed the last few games with an injury. Packers beat reporters all reported that the move is related to roster management and that the Packers expect Melton to remain in the organization on the practice squad in week one. Bo Melton will still play Sunday as a practice squad elevation and return to the 53 next week. This is a roster management move by the Packers. Not exactly sure why, but Melton will remain with the team. — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) September 11, 2026 There is some question about whether Melton can immediately re-sign with the Packers, however. Melton appears to have only three accrued seasons of NFL experience (defined as 6 or more games on full-pay status). That woould not qualify him for vested veteran status and would require that he clear waivers before the Packers can re-sign him to the practice squad. Should another NFL team claim him, the Packers would lose Melton entirely. With Melton currently on a league-minimum contract, he could feasibly be an intriguing target for other teams around the NFL, especially one that, for example, has a general manager, head coach, and quarterback who are familiar with him from their time in Green Bay over the last few years. Frankly, it would be a coup for the Miami Dolphins if they were to land Melton for free given their young and inexperienced stable of receivers and Melton’s familiarity with Malik Willis. Tom Silverstein, however, indicates that Melton is a vested veteran and therefore immediately becomes a free agent, which would allow him to immediately re-sign with the Packers’ practice squad. The Packers signed Melton away from the Seattle Seahawks’ practice squad late in the 2022 season, and he then spent most of the 2023 campaign on the Packers’ practice squad. However, he earned a callup to the active roster in November and exploded onto the scene with a 6-catch, 105-yard, game against the Minnesota Vikings on New Year’s Eve. That was the Packers’ first 100-yard receiving game by any player that season, and he continued his breakout a week late with another 62 yards on five receptions in the season finale while being on full-pay status for six games, thereby earning an accrued season for 2023. Melton then spent 2024 buried on the wide receiver depth chart as the team’s 5th/6th wideout, only catching 8 passes despite playing in every game and logging 251 offensive snaps, but he made a name for himself on the special teams units. Melton remained an option for the offense in 2025 after his formal switch to cornerback, and he still recorded 4 receptions for 107 yards, including a long touchdown in the Packers’ week 13 win over the Bears, while never actually taking a snap on defense. If Melton is indeed vested, then this makes some sense, but it still requires explanation. Why do the Packers need the roster spot? The team clearly is making space for some corresponding move, though that move has not yet been reported. Stay tuned for news that will hopefully explain why this move is happening, and why now is the time for it. UPDATE: Matt Schneidman further reports that Melton is, somehow, a vested veteran, and that there is no corresponding move to fill his spot on the 53-man roster. UPDATE: From APC’s own Justis Mosqueda in the comments section . Alright, here’s the info I have at this point: Wendell Ferreira’s information that Bo Melton was credited for four seasons (this changed this offseason; he was previously listed with three by the NFLPA) is true. Basically, there are two ways the NFL counts NFL tenure: accrued seasons and credited seasons. Accrued seasons means that you’re on the NFL’s active/inactive lists (including healthy scratches and scratches for injuries) for at least six weeks of a regular season. This impacts things like the exclusive rights/restricted free agent tenders a player can receive. Melton has two of these accrued seasons, as he only played in five games for the 2023 Packers and wasn’t on the field at all for his rookie season of 2022. This is why he’s four years into his NFL career but was only hit with the exclusive rights free-agent tender (typical for free agents coming out of their second season in the league). A credited season is when a player has been on the active/inactive roster for at least three games. This impacts things like whether a player is counted as a vested veteran for the waiver process or veteran termination pay. Melton has four of these because his 2022 season with the Packers (he was on the team for just two weeks) counted as a three-week stay. The reason for this is that players poached from practice squads (as Melton was from Seattle) receive a guaranteed three weeks’ worth of pay. So he was paid for three weeks, even though the Packers only had two weeks left in the regular season and missed the playoffs. Again, there was some debate about Melton’s credited seasons at one point this offseason, as the timing of his 2022 addition put him in a unique spot. It’s not often that a rookie Week 16 practice squad elevation in a non-playoff year plays between 2 and 5 games in his second year with the team and ends up making the roster three years down the line, putting this rule of a two-year accrued player and four-year credited player in play. Because Melton is credited with four seasons, Melton was allowed to be released by the Packers without subjecting him to waivers, which is why he was quickly picked up on the practice squad (Green Bay had a vacancy because defensive tackle Jaden Crumedy was claimed by the Houston Texans today ). Veteran termination pay (what people usually refer to as a veteran’s salary becoming guaranteed in Week 1) is based on credited seasons, which is almost certainly why the Packers made this move (on top of the practice squad vacancy). Moving forward, Green Bay will be able to release Melton from their 53-man roster (once he’s added back up) without penalty, whereas if they kept him on the 53-man roster, they would have been down about a million dollars minimum (assuming Melton filed for the once-in-career opportunity for termination pay). Thank you for reading about this hyper-niche roster move that will ultimately mean nothing when Melton plays on Sunday and is added back to the 53-man roster in the near future. It bothered me enough that I pestered people in the league about it on a Friday.

title: Packers Key to Victory: Chuck it deep
summary: Week 1 is weird for a variety of reasons. Teams change so much throughout the offseason – additions, subtractions, hiring, firings, turn turn turn – so looking at numbers/film from the previous season won’t always shed light on the current season. That being said, I was combing through some stats over at NFL Pro and […]
full_text: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 1 is weird for a variety of reasons. Teams change so much throughout the offseason – additions, subtractions, hiring, firings, turn turn turn – so looking at numbers/film from the previous season won’t always shed light on the current season. That being said, I was combing through some stats over at NFL Pro and found a handful of stats that could point to something to keep an eye on this week. The first stat is simple: last year, the Green Bay Packers were the 5th best team at deep passing (throws 20+ yards down the field. The Vikings were the 28th best defense at defending against the deep pass. That’s a good starting point. The Packers are better at passing deep than the Vikings are at defending it. The Vikings were much better at defending Short (#6) and Intermediate (#3) passing. Here’s the second stat: Jordan Love averaged 10.2 air yards per attempt with Christian Watson on the field last season, compared to 7.8 air yards per attempt when Watson was off the field. On the season, Love threw 5 TDs on throws 20+ yards down the field: 3 of those were to Watson & 1 of them was on a play with Watson on the field. That means Love threw only 1 deep TD all year without Watson on the field. The third stat basically just expands on the second one: Christian Watson averaged 17.6 air yards per target from Week 8 on last season, the second most amount among qualifying receivers during that span. Watson had 9 receptions on deep passes, most in the league during that stretch. Last but not least, there’s the matter of blitzing. We know how Brian Flores loves his blitzes. Last season, Jordan Love had an EPA per Play of +0.30 against the blitz, tied for best in the league with Matt Stafford (for reference, Drake Maye had the best overall EPA per Play last season at +0.25). Love’s time to throw when blitzed was 2.78, which means he wasn’t just looking for the quick option. Love’s Deep Throw % when blitzed of 13.2% was 5th in the league. His ability to drift away from pressure and throw off his back foot certainly helps with this, but he doesn’t really panic against a blitz. Football can be complicated, but it can also be simple. If a blitz is on the way, chuck it deep to Watson. Albums listened to: Julien Baker – Turn Out the Lights ; Brian Fallon – Not Bad for New Jersey

(Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers do appear to have game-time decisions on their hands with a pair of their starting offensive linemen. On Friday’s formal injury report for the team’s season opener against the Minnesota Vikings, the Packers have given both left guard Aaron Banks and right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele the questionable status. Bako-Bewele has been working through a knee issue and has been limited in practice all week. However, he did tell reporters earlier in the week that he expected to play on Sunday, and to play a full game. Meanwhile, Banks’ knee tendinitis has kept him in and out of practice throughout training camp and left him limited through this week’s practices as well. On the good news front, several other key Packers are expected to play and do not have an injury status for Sunday’s game. Left tackle Jordan Morgan is one of those players, having been limited on Wednesday with a knee issue but practiced fully the rest of the week. Meanwhile, key defensive pieces Barryn Sorrell, Javon Hargrave, and Devonte Wyatt were all limited throughout the week with various maladies but all have been given no injury status and should be good to go. The Vikings, meanwhile, have no players listed with any injury statuses on their report, giving them a full complement of players on their 53-man roster. title: Jordan Love is the least-sacked active NFL quarterback
summary: While looking through the Green Bay Packers’ 2025 stats to get ready for the start of the 2026 season, something interesting caught my eye. I noticed that in his 15 games last season, Packers quarterback Jordan Love was sacked merely 21 times, a sack rate of just 4.57%. That seemed pretty darn low to me, […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - SEPTEMBER 24: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers evades a tackle during the first half of an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2023 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images While looking through the Green Bay Packers’ 2025 stats to get ready for the start of the 2026 season, something interesting caught my eye. I noticed that in his 15 games last season, Packers quarterback Jordan Love was sacked merely 21 times, a sack rate of just 4.57%. That seemed pretty darn low to me, so I looked a bit deeper and found something that was surprised me even more. No active quarterback has been sacked on a lower rate of their dropbacks than Love over their careers. It’s a common refrain that sack rate is more of a quarterback statistic than an offensive line. Offensive lines allow pressure, but the quarterback has the ball in his hands and is the final determining factor on a sack. A quarterback can feel pressure coming and get the ball out quickly (either on target or via throwaways); he can navigate the pocket and avoid the pass rush; he can break tackles in the backfield and scramble to avoid sacks. Jordan Love, while not a truly elite athlete, does all of these things well, and he has been a top-10 quarterback in terms of minimizing sacks in each of his three seasons as the Packers’ starter. Notably, he usually gives his receivers a good chance to make a catch rather than just avoiding the rush and chucking the ball into the stands, like a certain Chicago Bears quarterback did last season. But it is impressive to note that Love’s consistency in sack avoidance is uncommon among NFL quarterbacks over his tenure. Love has finished no worse than 7th in sack rate and has been lower than 5% in each of the last three years, establishing a clear trend. Only two other players even did this twice in that span: Josh Allen and Bo Nix. After back-to-back top-two and sub-4% seasons in 2023 and 2024, Allen fell off harshly in 2025, reverting to a rookie season sack rate of 8%. Nix, meanwhile, has been elite in this area since arriving in the NFL; his 3.76% sack rate would be the active leader if he had been around long enough to qualify for the leaderboard, which should happen sometime during 2026. Looking at career numbers for qualifying quarterbacks — those with at least 1,500 pass attempts, according to Pro Football Reference — Love is the clear #1 among active players. His 4.27% sack rate beats 2nd-ranked Patrick Mahomes (4.46%), who has been hurt by significantly higher sack rates over the last two years. They’re the only two under 5% for their careers; next up on the list is Jared Goff, surprisingly, at number 3 with a rate of 5.19% (throwaways playing a part, perhaps?), followed by Allen at 5.30% and Tua Tagavailoa rounding out the top five at 5.50%. Love is in some pretty rarified air here, and it’s worth noting that Pro Football Reference’s leaderboard includes unofficial sack numbers from 1960 to 1981, after which when the sack officially became a stat, and AFL numbers as well. Love’s career rate ranks 7th all-time behind a top 6 of George Blanda, Peyton Manning, Dan Marino, Doug Williams, Mark Rypien, and Drew Brees. That’s an impressive group — each of those players is a Pro Football Hall of Famer, a Super Bowl-winning quarterback, or both. Notably, Love’s predecessor is much lower on these lists. Aaron Rodgers’ career sack rate is more than two full percentage points higher than Loves, at 6.42%. That puts him as a middle-of-the-pack player, ranking 18th among 34 qualifying active QBs and 89th out of 204 on the career leaderboard. Rodgers, famously, would rather have taken a sack than throw the ball into harm’s way. Love is less afraid of putting the ball up, but that tendency has served him well so far in his career; his accuracy on deep balls and under pressure is very good, and the EPA/play numbers love him for not just minimizing the negative plays, but also being able to generate some positives out of them. This is an important factor to keep in mind as the Packers head into a week one matchup with questions on the offensive line ahead of the blitz-happy Minnesota Vikings defense. If the Packers were putting a more sack-prone quarterback behind this line, optimism about Green Bay’s performance in this game would be tempered, but Love has proven that he is able to avoid sacks at a historically-good rate while still generating positive plays. He’ll need to do just that on Sunday if the Packers want to open the season 1-0.

title: Packers got help from long-time OL coach Harry Hiestand in camp
summary: The Packers’ offensive line got some additional help from a long-time college and pro offensive line coach. According to reporting from the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel’s Tom Silverstein, Harry Hiestand spent training camp with the Packers in what appeared to be a consultant-style role. Hiestand is about as decorated as an offensive line coach can be, […]
full_text: SOUTH BEND, IN - APRIL 23: Notre Dame Fighting Irish offensive line coach Harry Hiestand looks on during the Notre Dame Blue-Gold Spring Football Game on April 23, 2022 at Notre Dame Stadium in South Bend, IN. (Photo by Robin Alam/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Packers’ offensive line got some additional help from a long-time college and pro offensive line coach. According to reporting from the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel’s Tom Silverstein , Harry Hiestand spent training camp with the Packers in what appeared to be a consultant-style role. Hiestand is about as decorated as an offensive line coach can be, boasting success and connections to significant players at just about every stop in his multi-decade career. Dating back to the 1980s, Hiestand coached with eight different college programs and one NFL team, the Chicago Bears, in two different stints. From 2005 through 2009, Hiestand worked with the Bears under head coach Lovie Smith, then returned to Chicago under Matt Nagy in 2018, staying through the 2019 season. In between those two tours with the Bears, Hiestand had stops at Tennessee and Notre Dame, and the latter appointment probably explains how he ended up in Green Bay. His time with the Fighting Irish overlapped with Matt LaFleur’s one-year stint there, so Hiestand’s role with the Packers turns out to be not that much of a surprise. In football, even more so than other businesses, it’s about who you know as much as what you know. So what’s Hiestand up to in Green Bay? That’s not exactly clear, as Silverstein laid out. He characterizes Hiestand as a “consultant,” but it might be more complicated than that: The well-respected Hiestand coached on the field during training camp, taking over some of the duties Butkus, Gordon or a quality control coach would normally handle. It meant, instead of having one offensive line coach in charge, under the supervision of the offensive coordinator and head coach, the Packers had three line coaches, plus an offensive coordinator who used to be a line coach, in the linemen’s ears. Hiestand isn’t listed in any official capacity on the Packers’ website, and Silverstein reports that he may still be offering some kind of insight to the team during the season, but his exact role, if any, is a mystery. Still, with as many questions as the Packers are facing on the offensive line, having another voice in the room hardly seems like a bad thing. Whatever pointers Hiestand can offer are probably worth whatever trade offs arise when you shake things up a bit.

full_text: On the eve of their regular season debut, the Houston Texans have announced another significant injury. Rookie DT Kayden McDonald is apparently suffering from an ankle injury and will begin the regular season on injured reserve. Battle Red Blog’s Nickschwager noted McDonald’s appearance on the injury report yesterday, but a placement on IR is a new and rather sudden development. The Texans have placed Kayden McDonald on IR & signed Jaden Crumedy to the 53 man roster in a corresponding move. pic.twitter.com/JoE7xhOz1y — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) September 11, 2026 McDonald will now be inactive for the first four games of the 2026 regular season: vs. Buffalo Bills, vs. Cincinnati Bengals, @ Indianapolis Colts, and vs. Dallas Cowboys. He will be eligible to return for Houston’s match against the Tennessee Titans on October 11th. In the meantime, the Texans are signing DT Jaden Crumedy from the Green Bay Packers practice squad. Panthers draft Miss St DL Jaden Crumedy pic.twitter.com/YbiRio1op0 — John Ellis (@1PantherPlace) April 27, 2024 Houston Chronicle reporter Jonathan M. Alexander stated following the announcement, “McDonald suffered the injury in practice Wednesday, a league source said. He did not practice Thursday or Friday and wore a protective boot over his foot in the locker room” Kayden McDonald, despite being a rookie second-round pick, was fixing to have a significant impact on Houston’s dominant defensive line. He earned first team All-American honors while starting for Ohio State in 2025, and quickly ascended draft boards after establishing himself as one of the best run-stoppers in the 2026 NFL Draft. He had a lot of fans here at Battle Red Blog, and I even got the chance to ask him a question representing the Blog at the 2026 NFL Draft in Pittsburgh: Our very own @FizzyJoe got to ask a question of the Houston #Texans ' latest addition to the defense! Here's Joe Critz with Kayden McDonald. pic.twitter.com/LXoOkmAXKl — Battle Red Blog (@battleredblog) April 25, 2026 He finished his final collegiate season with 65(!) tackles, a preposterous stat for a beefy interior lineman, and his pass-rush seemed to be improving down the stretch. Fortunately for the Texans, they still have depth in the interior defensive line, with starting DTs Sheldon Rankins and Tommy Togiai still expected to absorb the majority of snaps. But, McDonald was brought in with the express purpose of being a run-stuffer who would contribute on early downs, something that could have pushed this defense to even greater heights. And, don’t look now, but there are currently four Texans defensive linemen on IR: McDonald, DE Dylan Horton, DE Solomon Byrd, and DE Ali Gaye. Fortunately, none of these players are starters, but depth at a pretty important spot on this year’s Texans team is now significantly thinner, especially during a fairly grizzly opening slate of games. We already know the Cowboys and Bills have great offenses, but the Bengals and Colts could both find themselves near to the top of the league in offensive production by year’s end, too. #Texans rookie defensive tackle Kayden McDonald is expected to return this season, per a league source, from an ankle injury he suffered in practice. A second-round draft pick from Ohio State and a former Big Ten Conference Defensive Lineman of the Year, McDonald can be… pic.twitter.com/kSzdhbxVCx — Aaron Wilson (@AaronWilson_NFL) September 11, 2026 Regardless, this Texans defense is one of the few groups in the league that can push through this wave of injuries relatively unscathed. Togiai, Mario Edwards Jr. and free-agent addition DT Logan Hall will have bigger roles this Sunday trying to contain defending NFL rushing leader RB James Cook, who ran for 116 yards and a touchdown at a piercing 6.8 Y/A against our mighty Texans defense in Week 12 last year. They’re hands will be very, very full this coming Sunday, but if there was a team able to take this blow and keep charging forward, it’s this Texans team! What do you think of this news? Are the Texans in more danger of losing their first game of the season because of this injury, or was McDonald just going to play a small role? Will new DT Jaden Crumedy surprise us all and make some sweet tackles in Week 1, or will Logan Hall have a banner game to start his Texans tenure? Let us know your thoughts down in the comments below! Go Texans!

title: Battle Red Blog Regular Season Power Rankings: 2026 Season
summary: Football is back! Every year here at Battle Red Blog, I spend some time every week gathering all of the Power Rankings pundits’ thoughts on the Houston Texans and relaying them here (of course, with some of my own thoughts sprinkled in). But, at the beginning of every season, I try to put together my […]
full_text: Football is back! Every year here at Battle Red Blog, I spend some time every week gathering all of the Power Rankings pundits’ thoughts on the Houston Texans and relaying them here (of course, with some of my own thoughts sprinkled in). But, at the beginning of every season, I try to put together my own personal power rankings, where I rank all 32 NFL teams, give a quick review of what I expect out of them this season, and predict their final regular season record. It’s may not come with as much cutting-edge analysis or data, but my rankings will be fun to look back on when they’re all wrong in a few months! Without further ado, here’s my 2026 NFL Power Rankings to start the NFL Season: 32. Cleveland Browns 2025 Record: 5-12 Notable Arrivals: T/G Tytus Howard T Spencer Fano (Rookie) LB Quincy Williams Notable Departures: DE Myles Garrett OG Wyatt Teller LB Devin Bush Once upon a time, Cleveland Browns 2026 Week 1 starting quarterback Deshaun Watson was the franchise savior for the Houston Texans. Now synonymous with the term “bust” in the NFL, Watson had an exceptional run as Houston’s starting signal-caller from 2017-2020, often recalled as some of successful yet fractious eras in Houston’s history. Former head coach/general manager Bill O’Brien was the ringleader of the Texans circus that Watson quarterbacked, but following O’Brien’s firing during a disastrous 2020 season, a lawsuit alleging extensive and shocking acts of sexual assault against Watson in early 2021 – that he originally swore to fight (to “clear his name”) only to settle in 2023 – as well his trade request following contract disputes with Houston, his fame in the city and in the world of sports took an unprecedented nose dive. Now in his fifth and final year of a gigantic, $250-million contract with the Cleveland Browns, Watson’s star has only continued to fade under Ohio skies and has often become the face of this woebegone era of the franchise. He reportedly barely won the starting job over second-year QB Shedeur Sanders despite being a highly paid veteran, and his open detest of the team’s supporters has practically earned him the honor of being a pariah in his own stadium. Watson just seemed to continuously sink further below the bar of what is deemed acceptable of a NFL quarterback throughout his half-decade in Cleveland, matching his zenith on the gridiron in Houston with piercing infamy in his new home. This year will be his last chance to turn it all around and prove to everyone that he can still be a competent NFL professional, but I sincerely doubt it. In front of him, Cleveland hopes to have a more consistent o-line – highlighted by the offseason signing former Texan RT/LG Tytus Howard and 2026 9th overall pick T Spencer Fano – as well as a better rushing attack with RB Quinshon Judkins back from injury. WRs Jerry Jeudy and rookies KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston could make an intriguing combination to pair with TE Harold Fannin Jr., but they’ll need the QB to be consistent, which is wishing upon a star. Defense, as it often the case with Cleveland in this new era, their lone saving grace from being by far the worst team in football. But, even here, a decline will likely occur considering superstar DE Myles Garrett has been traded to the Los Angeles Rams. The Browns got DE Jared Verse in return, but he can only hope to fill half of the hole Garrett leaves. If DT Mason Graham can start realizing his draft hype, they might have a new young-duo up front, but they can only do so much. Cleveland does have some talent behind the line with reigning defensive rookie of the year LB Carson Scheswinger, LB Quincy Williams, CB Denzel Ward, and S Grant Delpit, who all will combine to create a strong backfield both against the run and against the pass. But, the big question mark at QB makes this season feel like a primer to the Arch Manning sweepstakes at the 2027 NFL Draft. Projected 2026 Record: 3-14 31. Miami Dolphins 2025 Record: 7-10 Notable Arrivals: QB Malik Willis CB Darrell Baker Jr. T Kadyn Proctor (Rookie) Notable Departures: QB Tua Tagovailoa WR Jaylen Waddle LB Bradley Chubb Like many other regimes in Miami, the Mike McDaniel era ended after just over three seasons at the helm. WR Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle are gone, QB Tua Tagovailoa is now the week one starter for Atlanta, and in his place is former Green Bay Packers’ backup QB Malik Willis. With new general manager Jon Eric-Sullivan and head coach Jeff Hafley committed to bringing some of that special Packers’ spice down south, the Dolphins will be trying to emulate a sort of smashmouth-esque offense complemented by an aggresive, ball-hawking defense. Miami’s offense will run through De’Von Achane, but in order for that to work, they’ll need a much better effort from 2025 second-rounder G Jonah Savaiinaea in his sophomore campaign as well as the entire tight end’s room to perform above expectations. Additionally, if their defense hopes to improve beyond their 24th-overall ranking last year, they’re going to need exceptional seasons from CB Jason Marshall Jr., and rookies Chris Johnson and S Michael Taaffe. Simply put, many positions on the Dolphins’ starting lineup are occupied by young and/or inexperienced players. They’ll be betting heavily on unknown prospects at multiple positions on both offense and defense, so…they’re tanking. The Miami Dolphins, despite having some intriguing players on the roster, did little this offseason to make them a better team than they were last year. If all of their young starters and rookies hit their ceiling in 2026, they have a chance to be interesting in December, but if not, they’ll be in the quarterback sweepstakes in April. Projected Record: 5-12 30. New York Jets 2025 Record: 3-14 Notable Arrivals: QB Geno Smith LB Demario Davis DE Joseph Ossai Notable Departures: S Tony Adams LB Jermaine Johnson G John Simpson How do you stay this bad for this long? I’ve ranked the Dolphins and Browns below the New York Jets for these power rankings, but at least both of those teams have appeared in the playoffs more than once in the last six years. Even the lowly Browns can lay claim to more playoff success than the Jets, who haven’t even sniffed the playoffs since 2011. It’s truly remarkable how this football team has practiced mediocrity with so many different coaches, general managers, quarterbacks, and more. This year’s rendition is led by second-year head coach Aaron Glenn, a former CB for the Jets who can now lay claim to NFL infamy for leading the very first defense in recorded history to finish the season with 0 interceptions. Isn’t it just poetic? It can’t get any worse than this, though. The only way to go is up for the defense, and they’ll do just that with new CB Nashon Wright and Ss Minkah Fitzpatrick and Dane Belton to complement Brandon Stephens. They’ll also be boosted by a completely remade defensive front, now manned by rookie second-overall pick David Bailey, trade acquisitions DTs Harrison Phillips and T’Vondre Sweat, and returning DE Will Macdonald IV. Big moves from a Jets front office that is appearing just as trade-happy as the previous, Joe Douglas-led regime, but don’t tell that to a Jets fan. It’s unlikely they’ll dig far out of the abyss they fell in last year, but the Jets should at least look competent on defense this year. On offense, QB Geno Smith’s long, winding journey back to the Jets starting job since losing it in 2015 makes for a good story to start the season with, but I’m trepidatious to say that it’ll be a success. WRs Garrett Wilson, Adonai Mitchell, rookie Omar Cooper Jr., and RB Breece Hall should give Geno enough weapons to be productive, but the o-line still has a lot to prove. Either way, Geno should be a better passer than Justin Fields was last year, but I wouldn’t bet on all of these spare parts gelling well right away. There might be some good Jets-related action by November or December, but their season will already be over by then.…

title: Five Good Texans questions with Buffalo Ramblings
summary: The NFL scheduling has its quirks and in one of those quirks, the Texans and the Bills match up for the third season in a row. The Texans owned Josh Allen in the first two matchups, but we will have to see if that happens yet again. A new season also marks a new opportunity […]
full_text: The NFL scheduling has its quirks and in one of those quirks, the Texans and the Bills match up for the third season in a row. The Texans owned Josh Allen in the first two matchups, but we will have to see if that happens yet again. A new season also marks a new opportunity to catch up with our comrades at the other sites. Matthew Byham has always been a joy to work with. We caught up with him to check in on the Bills before Sunday. Battle Red Blog: The Bills achieved a lot of success under Sean McDermott but it ultimately wasn’t enough. Why do you think he came up short? Matthew Bynum: Sean McDermott accomplished so much as head coach of the Bills that it feels a bit unfair to say he came up short. But he did, simply because his teams never did win an AFC Championship Game, nor play in or (better) win a Super Bowl. It’s a small but significant list of items McDermott didn’t check off after nine seasons. McDermott and general manager Brandon Beane built teams to take down the Kansas City Chiefs. Yet every time they faced KC in the playoffs, they lost despite Josh Allen playing out of his mind most of the time. McDermott came up short because he was never the best coach in playoff games against the Chiefs. That’s enough, and a lot, but that’s not all there is to it. A very demanding coach, McDermott’s defensive scheme relied on intelligence, both individually and as a unit. Players had to be system sound in their assignments at all times, or else disaster would strike. Yet there was also a focus on a player’s RAS score. That meant trying to make it all work with two often diametrically unique types of player skill sets — the heady leader, and the instinctual athletic freak. Sure, anyone coaching an NFL team would welcome superlatives from both arenas, but McDermott relied on players being able to excel from both buckets whether or not they were capable. SB Nation’s new app is perfect for game day! SB Nation’s NEW game chat feature in the app is perfect for keeping the latest Texans updates and conversations at your fingertips. Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Too often, McDermott’s defense proved to be the team’s playoff Achilles heel. Not always, and in no way is the offense’s failures in more than one playoff game’s final drive overlooked. But the head coach was a defensive mind and his units faltered in the biggest moments. Time also worked against McDermott. Nearly a decade at the helm is a long time in the NFL. The reason people remember long NFL tenures is because it’s so rare. But McDermott-coached teams hold the best regular-season record in that span. You don’t just move on from a guy because he didn’t get lucky enough to play and win a Super Bowl. Well, at least not until missing out becomes a trauma-filled trend. The Bills have a large number of catch phrases attached to their worst moments, and McDermott owns many of them. When someone mentions “13 seconds” anyone who follows the sport immediately drifts to Buffalo’s gut-wrenching overtime loss against the Kansas City Chiefs. Many thought a change should have been made after that loss. But a lot of leeway was given simply because it was Andy Reid and Patrick Mahomes. It wasn’t yet time. The trouble is that things didn’t meaningfully improve with time. With Allen, McDermott’s teams were a perennial playoff participant, and a Super Bowl favorite. The postseason was expected, all but guaranteed. Yet McDermott never could find a way toward earning the one seed. His teams were always forced to play on Wild Card Weekend, to the detriment of a severely injured defensive roster. You’d think that if the playoffs appeared automatic, then a lot of effort would be spent on the team’s second season. But too often if felt like the only one who showed up to play was Allen. That’s unacceptable, no matter how good Allen is. They were dog-walked at home against the Cincinnati Bengals the year after 13 seconds — the same season Damar Hamlin almost died playing against those same Bengals. McDermott managed Hamlin’s trauma well, but that clearly didn’t extend into the postseason. By and large, he should be given a pass for that, but it’s the same game where the Diggs-Allen drama gained legs. Then there was the home loss to the Chiefs the next season, which saw McDermott settle for a field goal try that wouldn’t have given them a win anyway. Instead, Buffalo missed another kick wide right (yup), and an over-matched defense folded while allowing Mahomes and company to win its first road playoff game. Whatever a person believes or doesn’t about last season’s loss to the Broncos, the fact is that the Bills were short-handed on defense thanks to McDermott’s decision to play then-rookie cornerback Maxwell Hairston Week 18. That resulted in an injury for Hairston during the closing minutes, which kept him out of postseason play. Sean Payton diagnosed an obvious weakness following an injury to Tre’Davious White that had Dane Jackson playing for Hairston, and it resulted in a touchdown. It’s not McDermott’s fault that the referees saw things a certain way to call the game as they did. It’s McDermott’s fault that his defense was ill-equipped to overcome injury. If I had to guess what really happened on an acute level, it’s that McDermott probably lost the locker room. That was perhaps true years earlier (specifically Diggs), but it’s difficult to move on easily from a coach who’s automatic in the regular season. Then there’s what co-owner Terry Pegula mentioned, seeing Allen beside himself. It may be that he’d seen enough and decided the franchise’s most prolific player was beginning to run out of time due to wasted opportunities. BRB: It’s a new era of Bills football with a new coach and new stadium. What changes are you expecting under Joe Brady? MB: Well, we’ve been told that the vibe is more relaxed, looser at One Bills Drive. Brady is the youngest head coach in the NFL, and by all accounts he’s a player’s coach who brings a more youthful and energetic swagger. He also comes from Sean Payton’s school of hard knocks (yes, that’s a sleight Payton’s way). No Brady is not a direct clone of Payton, but it would be silly to think he won’t lean on Payton’s leadership example while trying to find his groove. He also has John Fox to help guide him, but Brady’s familiarity with the offense should benefit his transition. I don’t necessarily expect a huge dynamic shift on offense, and it’s likely we’ll have to wait and see what the offense abandons and adds to know where he and McDermott differed. How much do you change for an offense that just finished top-three in the NFL last season? I do expect to see running back James Cook III more involved in the passing game. He came out of college dubbed a bona fide dual-threat player, but for the most part his usage there has been as a distant second fiddle. Time will tell if Brady allows Allen to do as he pleases as a run, and if he leans more heavily into the types of west coast scheme Payton teaches. BRB: Obviously championship windows are about the quarterback. Can you make your best case for Josh Allen to return to MVP Allen? MB: I guess my move is to offer up that I see zero need for Allen to reascend to an MVP level simply because I still see him playing at that level. Without Allen, the Bills are fighting with the Jets for a spot in the AFC’s basement each season. Allen raises everyone’s play around him, which included a less-than-stellar wide receivers room last season. All that Buffalo needs is competent play around Allen come playoff time. Otherwise, any MVP-worthy season by Allen will once again be little more than a regular-season award. But to honor your ask here, I suppose I see Allen winning the MVP if he puts together a season similar to or better than his 2024 campaign, while guiding the team to greater success under a rookie head coach. title: Here’s how the Colts can start 1-0
summary: 1-0 is a great sight for NFL fans. It is the validation that your hopes and dreams might be well placed. It also starts a team on the right track statistically to make the postseason and avoids the dreaded 0-2 hole to start the season. It isn’t a panacea, as things can go sideways, but […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 11: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates a touchdown during the first quarter in a game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on October 11, 2021 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Rob Carr/Getty Images) | Getty Images 1-0 is a great sight for NFL fans. It is the validation that your hopes and dreams might be well placed. It also starts a team on the right track statistically to make the postseason and avoids the dreaded 0-2 hole to start the season. It isn’t a panacea, as things can go sideways, but it feels pretty good. Here is how the Indianapolis Colts can get it done. The Ravens are a good team, so it won’t be an easy task. The Colts have some advantages, however. The home crowd will be back and ready. It hasn’t always translated into Week One wins, but the confines of Lucas Oil are much more advantageous than a road opener. The Colts are also trending towards good health. Daniel Jones is back, and Alec Pierce should be ready as well. The bumps and bruises of camp are also healing for Tyler Warren and Josh Downs. Jonathan Taylor is the bell cow, and the Ravens will have their hands full trying to contain him. If the Colts can establish the run game early, Taylor may prove to be too much for the Ravens late. A lot of Sunday’s success will come down to how well the defense contains Lamar Jackson. Jackson is electric. If they can keep him in the pocket, though, that electricity falls a few wattages. Speaking of a bell cow, Derrick Henry is in the backfield for the Ravens. Stopping the dual threat of he and Jackson will be tough, but it’s also the key to victory. The defense has some question marks. Veterans have returned to form, but the effectiveness of the line remains in the air. Young linebackers will be tested as well. If those units rise to the occasion, they can keep the Colts’ offense in position to win. Looking back at Week Ones for the Colts is troubling, so let’s not look back too far. How about one year? The Colts got off to a hot start by using the momentum of a win to start the season. The offense needs to find the footing that was lost in the back half of 2025, and the Colts need to control the line of scrimmage on defense. Do those things and the Colts will start 2026 with that coveted 1-0.
