title: Canal Street Chronicles welcomes new writer, Andrew Lotz
summary: Hi, my name is Andrew Lotz and I’m the newest contributing writer for the Canal Street Chronicles as well as And The Valley Shook. As a lifelong football obsessive, this opportunity immediately jumped out at me, and I couldn’t be more excited to begin covering my two favorite teams in all of sports, the New […]
full_text: Hi, my name is Andrew Lotz and I’m the newest contributing writer for the Canal Street Chronicles as well as And The Valley Shook. As a lifelong football obsessive, this opportunity immediately jumped out at me, and I couldn’t be more excited to begin covering my two favorite teams in all of sports, the New Orleans Saints and LSU Tigers. Growing Up My love for football began as a member of the Versailles Cardinals while I attended St. Mark Catholic School in Chalmette. Strip sacking a Carolyn Park quarterback at the ripe age of 5 was the exact moment I knew I liked this game and wanted to be the next Rickey Williams (Prime Run Ricky Run days). As a proud native of THE St. Bernard Parish, when my family decided to relocate to the DFW area after Katrina, my love for football was heightened as I was now able to embrace the outsider role amidst all the Cowboys fans that surrounded me on a daily basis. I also quickly learned that Texas football is as serious as advertised and quickly joined the year-round rotation of tackle in the fall and flag in the spring. Luckily for me, my baseball background melded nicely with my new favorite sport as by the age of 9, I was the quarterback for my local “Cowboys” youth team. Through the years I was lucky enough to keep working to get better and eventually became the starting quarterback at my high school for my junior and senior years. A Team Sport High School football was where I really began to cultivate relationships around the game of football which have evolved into lifelong friendships. The team dynamic became my favorite part of playing as we were constantly preached to about how the true beauty of football is the requirement of all 11 players on the field to work together at all times and embrace unselfishness for the greater good of the team. This theme was easy to understand as I had watched Drew Brees live that ethos and carry my hometown team through the most successful run in Saints history. Furthered Education At LSU football summer camp as a freshman in high school, Les Miles gave a speech that changed the way I looked at life. The quote from Coach Miles that stuck with me as a highly competitive adolescent was, “You should compete harder in the classroom than on the football field” which lit a fire in my otherwise absent intellectual curiosity. From that day on my competitive spirit led me to a love and appreciation for multiple subjects with math at the top of the list. In college, that interest in math and desire to work in a creative field led me to pursue and obtain a bachelor’s degree in information systems and a master’s degree in data Analytics, both from Texas Lutheran University where I played quarterback and some tight end throughout my 4 seasons with the team. Football as an Adult At TLU, I was blessed to be coached by some very smart coaches over a 5-year span and developed a love for learning about the game and every facet of how a team operates. In my final year of graduate school, I became an offensive assistant for the football team and began to set my sights on a professional career in the football world. Throughout my professional career, the itch to be involved with the game carried me to Houston where I worked on the business side of the Texans organization followed by an assistant role in TCU’’s recruiting and scouting department. After spending a season strictly as a fan, the constant desire to be involved in the game has now led me to CSC and ATV and I couldn’t be more excited for the opportunity. I look forward to being able to share my passions for football, creativity, and continuous learning while also dusting the cobwebs off writing skills that haven’t seen much action since an intro to creative writing class circa 2016. Who Dat & Geaux Tigers!

title: Interview with the Enemy: Detroit Lions
summary: This Sunday, the New Orleans Saints will head to Ford Field to face the Detroit Lions in the 2026 regular season opener. To break it down, Ryan Mathews of Pride of Detroit joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: While the culture and competitive standards in Detroit have undeniably improved since Dan Campbell arrived in 2021, if […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 18: Donovan Ezeiruaku #6 of the Dallas Cowboys pulls off Taliese Fuaga #75 of the New Orleans Saints helmet during joint practice at River Ridge Playing Fields on August 18, 2026 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images This Sunday, the New Orleans Saints will head to Ford Field to face the Detroit Lions in the 2026 regular season opener. To break it down, Ryan Mathews of Pride of Detroit joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: While the culture and competitive standards in Detroit have undeniably improved since Dan Campbell arrived in 2021, if the Lions fail to get over the hump again, could his seat potentially start to get hot? RM: Detroit had steadily been improving, year after year, since Dan Campbell took over as head coach of the Lions in 2021, but last season was ultimately a step back. The team floundered down the stretch, losing four of their final six games, but the 9-8 record was just the ninth winning season the Lions have posted since the year 2000—four of those have happened under Campbell’s tutelage. If the Lions return to the playoffs this season, his seat is as cool as the peanut butter and jelly sandwich your mother packed on top of the freezer pack for lunch. If the Lions miss the playoffs for a second year in a row, well, things might get to heating up for Detroit’s most successful head coach this century. NJ: Who are some notable names who will be sidelined for the Lions on Sunday against the Saints? RM: Much of the self loathing from fans in Detroit about the Lions comes from opining why injuries plague this franchise unlike any other team in the NFL. It’s true the injury bug has bitten them—so badly in 2024 that it’s become the inflection point for news of every injury since—but everyone’s got their own injury problems. Detroit comes into this matchup without their two starting safeties from a year ago. It’s unclear whether former All-Pro Kerby Joseph will ever play football again, Brian Branch is also on the PUP list after tearing his Achilles in December of last year, but there’s definitely been more encouraging updates about his progress back from injury. Still, being down a couple of playmaking safeties will challenge the veterans they brought in to replace them: Chuck Clark and Avonte Maddox. The Lions will also be without center Cade Mays, their big free-agent signing of the offseason, so they’ll need to rely on their return in the David Montgomery trade, interior offensive lineman Juice Scruggs. The good news for Detroit is all of these injuries were known in early August, and that’s given them ample time to prepare their depth for starting roles. NJ: What are some areas that New Orleans could potentially exploit based on what you saw from Detroit during training camp and throughout the preseason? RM: There’s at least one area on each side of the ball that I need to see before I believe. On defense, it’s Detroit’s ability to marry their coverage and pass rush more consistently. The Lions were able to get teams into third down last season, and did a decent enough job in getting off the field—Detroit had the ninth-best third-down conversion rate against in 2025—but they allowed far too many big plays against them on third-and-long. Detroit finished with the third-worst time to pressure a year ago, but it looks like the Lions are going to get a bit more aggressive when it comes to their pass-rush plan based on their 53-man roster. Over on the other side of the ball, it’s all about the offensive line. Detroit’s offense has long prided itself on being tougher and more physical up front than their opponents, running the ball to help set up opportunities in the pass game. Their identity strayed a bit last year, seeing their success rate in the run game take a dip from 61.1% in 2024 to 54.7% in 2025. General manager Brad Holmes has poured a ton of resources this offseason into rebuilding that offensive line, signing the aforementioned Cade Mays (who, again, will not play in this one) and drafting Blake Miller in the first round of the 2026 NFL Draft. Last season, the Lions offensive line looked absolutely lost in their season opener against the Green Bay Packers, but this time they’re at home for this debut against the Saints. If the Saints can match the intensity and physicality of the Lions’ offense, there’s room for New Orleans to make this one interesting. NJ: Who is one Lions player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Sunday—someone who may not receive much national attention but could have a strong performance? RM: Since it’s Week 1, it’s hard to gauge just how much playing time certain players, especially those tucked away on the depth chart, might get from the jump. But Campbell and the rest of the coaching staff have raved about the defensive line, and sixth-round rookie Skyler Gill-Howard was a huge standout this summer in Allen Park. He’s a penetrating defensive tackle who knows how to get skinny and slip past offensive linemen, and he’s got some freaky athleticism to boot, so he could be part of Detroit’s pass-rush plan as early as this week. NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Lions (-340) are currently 6.5-point favorites over the Saints (+275) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction? RM: The Saints are a really interesting team that, at full strength, seem like they could challenge for that NFC South crown this season. The Lions, however, are still one of the elite teams in the NFL. If this game was in New Orleans, there’d be more room for an upset, but Ford Field is a pretty raucous environment to walk into for this Saints team. Detroit wins this one, 31-17. Thank you again to Ryan Mathews for joining us to preview this week’s matchup! You can check out the rest of his work here .

title: Our defense vs. their offense: Detroit Lions
summary: On Sunday, both the New Orleans Saints and Detroit Lions will begin their 2026 regular season at Ford Field as a long offseason comes to a conclusion. Ahead of what will likely be a competitive NFC battle, let’s take a look at what the New Orleans defense will be up against this weekend. Saints’ defensive […]
full_text: On Sunday, both the New Orleans Saints and Detroit Lions will begin their 2026 regular season at Ford Field as a long offseason comes to a conclusion. Ahead of what will likely be a competitive NFC battle, let’s take a look at what the New Orleans defense will be up against this weekend. Saints’ defensive coordinator Brandon Staley lost a couple of key pieces from his 2025 group. Talented veteran players such as CB Alontae Taylor and LB Demario Davis departed from the Big Easy by way of the free agency market. While New Orleans has young guys with potential on the current roster, it is difficult to replicate the vocal nature and consistent presence these leaders provided. While areas on the defense remain weak, the Saints have made some key additions on top of retaining All-Pro DE Cam Jordan. LB Kaden Elliss and DT Christen Miller made their way to New Orleans via free agency and this year’s NFL draft, respectively. With Jordan still recovering from a hamstring injury sustained late in the offseason, it will be critical for New Orleans to get some pressure on Lions’ QB Jared Goff while keeping their offense backed into long down-and-distance situations. Detroit has explosive playmakers at just about every offensive skill position. Sharing the backfield with Goff, tailback Jahmyr Gibbs can attack defenses both in the run and passing games. The Lions also possess one of the better WR duos in the league with Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams, but just when you think everyone is covered, TE Sam LaPorta can stretch the field and make a linebacker look silly. Last year, the Lions had a top five offense in the league averaging just under 375 yards per game. When your offense has the capabilities of moving the football up and down the field like Detroit does, putting points on the board becomes much easier. Detroit scored an average of 28.3 (Saints fans laugh here) points a contest in 2025. If New Orleans expects to have any shot at overcoming the Lions on the road, their defense will have to anchor down and disrupt an offense that can find a rhythm quickly.

title: Week 1 Prediction: New Orleans Saints vs. Detroit Lions
summary: There’s no easing into the 2026 season for the New Orleans Saints. They will open the season on Sunday afternoon on the road against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field, facing a team that is very eager to put last year’s disappointing 9-8 record behind it. For the Saints, it’s an opportunity to show just […]
full_text: There’s no easing into the 2026 season for the New Orleans Saints. They will open the season on Sunday afternoon on the road against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field, facing a team that is very eager to put last year’s disappointing 9-8 record behind it. For the Saints, it’s an opportunity to show just how much progress they’ve made entering Year 2 under head coach Kellen Moore. New Orleans finished 6-11 a year ago, but the team closed the season with four wins in its final five games and enters 2026 with considerably higher expectations. Quarterback Tyler Shough has emerged as a leader, while the Saints made several offseason additions designed to give him more help. But the Saints will have their work cut out for them Sunday. Detroit is a difficult place to open a season, and the Lions have plenty of firepower on both sides of the football. Aidan Hutchinson is coming off a career-high 14.5-sack season, establishing himself as one of the NFL’s top edge rushers and earning second-team All-Pro honors. The Saints also won’t have a completely healthy roster. Running back Alvin Kamara, who has been limited in practice all week, could miss the opener with an MCL injury, meaning offseason addition Travis Etienne will be taking on a significant workload. First-round wide receiver Jordyn Tyson will also miss the first four games after landing on injured reserve with a hamstring injury. Defensively, New Orleans will be without defensive end Cam Jordan, who is battling a hamstring injury and was ruled out Wednesday as well as defensive tackle Bryan Bresee, who was placed on injured reserve in early August. Still, there are several reasons to believe the Saints can make this interesting. Detroit will also be without two key defensive backs, Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, who will miss at least the first four games as well as the uncertainty of DB Christian Izien, DE Derrick Moore and DL Mekhi Wingo, who have all been limited this week in practice. That could give Shough some opportunities to attack a secondary that isn’t at full strength. The biggest question for New Orleans may be whether the offensive line can protect Shough and whether the Saints can establish enough of a running game to keep Hutchinson and the Lions’ pass rush from taking over. If they can, I expect this to be a competitive game into the fourth quarter. Detroit has the home-field advantage, a talented offense and a defense capable of creating problems for a young New Orleans offense. The Lions are favored by 6.5 points entering the week, and I think they find a way to make enough plays late. Prediction: Lions 27 – Saints 24 However, if Tyler Shough proves capable of making the big throws in a hostile environment, New Orleans could quickly make it clear that this is a very different team from the one that finished 6-11 last season. title: New York Giants mailbag: Defensive alignments, expectations as season begins
summary: Richard Vitto asks: I was hoping you could clarify how the defensive line actually gets set up. Most of the time it seems to me that they play only 2 down linemen with 4 linebackers. Maybe to start a game or a possession they use a true front seven but without really tracking I really […]
full_text: Richard Vitto asks: I was hoping you could clarify how the defensive line actually gets set up. Most of the time it seems to me that they play only 2 down linemen with 4 linebackers. Maybe to start a game or a possession they use a true front seven but without really tracking I really don’t think I see it that often. Can you give us a general sense of how often they are in a package with just 2 down linemen and extra dbacks? And when they are on that configuration who are the “starters” most often on the field? Ed says: Richard, I could find and quote you numbers from last season. That, though, is pointless because the Giants have a new defensive coordinator and much different defensive personnel. The “base” defense is considered a 3-4, with three down linemen with their hands in the ground. Again, though, that is kind of pointless. You will see some occasions where the Giants line up that way. You will see occasions where they line up with two down linemen and everyone else standing. You will see occasions where two edge defenders function as hand in the ground defensive ends, making the defense look like a traditional four-man front. You will see times when there is only one true defensive lineman. You will see times when there are none and an edge defender (probably Kayvon Thibodeaux) functions as a pass-rushing nose tackle. Teams play defense nowadays according to down-and-distance, game score, and the game clock. It is all situational. It is impossible to give you numbers on how often different packages are used until we actually see it. That said, the guys I would consider true starters in the front are D.J. Reader, Shelby Harris, Arvell Reese, Tremaine Edmunds, Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, and Thibodeaux. The safeties are Jevon Holland and Tyler Nubin. Dru Phillips is the nickel cornerback. I couldn’t tell you who the Giants will decided to start at the outside cornberbacks slots — it is some combination of Greg Newsome, Deonte Banks, Paulson Adebo. John Brenner asks: It seems to me that the Giants have developed a troubling pattern over the last 10 or 15 years of not looking ready to play at the beginning of the season. I don’t have the numbers in front of me, but my impression is that they’ve lost the overwhelming majority of their openers and several times they haven’t just lost, but have looked completely unprepared. Do the numbers and your own observations support that impression? If so, what do you think has caused it across different coaches and rosters? And do you see any reason to expect something different against Dallas on Sunday under John Harbaugh? Ed says: John, have you not been reading the website? We have been covering this topic for months. In fact, we have been talking about it for years. I asked Brian Daboll about it before both the 2024 and 2025 seasons. Most recently, it was addressed in this post . Peter Smyth asks: This last week has been fan-torture. I can’t wait for this long, (but hope-filled), offseason to end and find out how good this team really is. National media, and even local writers and hosts are tempering expectations and predict slight or medium improvement. Often, they sound like they haven’t been paying attention to our team and are just writing us off. As a BBV zealot, I have convinced myself the G-men will go on a run this season like Washington in 2024 and the Pats in 2025. I’m asking you to be my Giants-fan-therapist. Am I nuts to strongly think this could be our year? Even a Super Bowl victory? Help me! Ed says: Peter, you are certainly encouraged to be as optimistic as you want to be. Something I keep saying, though, is that the kind of one-year turnaround the New England Patriots and Chicago Bears experienced last season are still the exception rather than the rule. I think if that is what you “expecting” in 2026, you are setting yourself up for disappointment. Maybe it happens. I just wouldn’t expect it to happen. When I made my game-by-game predictions, the most optimistic predicition I could make is 9-8. I still believe that. Maybe the Giants win six games. Maybe everything falls their way, and they get into double-digits in the win column. I feel better about this team because I know the track record of the guy who is now in charge. I just can’t expect an overnight miracle. There is still a lot to be proven, and a lot of work to be done. Doug Mollin asks: Saw a stat from Sharp Football that really caught my eye. “The Giants were leading in games last year for more snaps than the following teams: Ravens, Chiefs, Bengals, Panthers, Vikings, Cowboys, Commanders, Browns, Buccaneers, Saints.” The Giants were leading in games last year for more snaps than the following teams: Ravens, Chiefs, Bengals, Panthers, Vikings, Cowboys, Commanders, Browns, Buccaneers, Saints per @SharpFootball A stat that boggles my mind and should give us hope for better results in 2026 pic.twitter.com/v7k3p66kpc — Justin Penik (@JustinPenik) September 8, 2026 Along with blowing 5 double digit fourth-quarter leads, it really makes me think the Giants could make a bigger leap this year than many expect. Could have had 7 wins last year with a little better luck, better coaching, better execution. What chance do you give the Giants to surprise on the upside over the predicted 7 win total? Is 10 wins out of the question? Ed says: Doug, as I said above, it’s not out of the question. Neither, though, is being a six-win team. As I said above, I just wouldn’t go into the season believing that it is automatic that John Harbaugh is going to turn the Giants into a 13-win team right away. Art Stein asks: To your knowledge is there any exchange of information or knowledge between the Giants and Rutgers. Historically, do coaches from Rutgers ask questions or seek information from the Giants? Ed says: Art, I don’t know what kind of information you think Rutgers coaches might seek from the Giants. To my knowledge, there isn’t anything other than the standard exchange of information about NFL Draft prospects. John McGruther asks: Do you know any of the words which the offense are using for their play calls and instructions, under the new coaching staff? I always remember “Omaha” being heard in the Manning years. Ed says: John, if I did that would be a problem. The rest of the NFL would know them, too. Submit a question Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

title: NY Giants news: John Harbaugh era set to begin, Matt Nagy, Brian Burns more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to as the John Harbaugh Era starts tomorrow. John Harbaugh not leaving anything to chance as his Giants era begins | The Record This was the early evening before the New York Giants began training camp at The Greenbrier Resort and John Harbaugh was walking […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to as the John Harbaugh Era starts tomorrow. John Harbaugh not leaving anything to chance as his Giants era begins | The Record This was the early evening before the New York Giants began training camp at The Greenbrier Resort and John Harbaugh was walking the grounds for the first time. The head coach and several team officials were admiring the picturesque setting with the mountains of West Virginia as the backdrop when someone half-jokingly suggested that the practice fields looked longer than 120 yards. Harbaugh on why Giants were the right fit Harbs Weekly: Time to get a gauge on the Giants | Giants.com Q: That was the start of his era with you, and now the same begins with Jaxson Dart. Where is the line between the importance of the quarterback-head coach relationship and him just being one of 53 on the roster? Harbaugh: To me it’s both, but everybody understands it. He is one of 53. He’s part of the team. He’s a teammate. He’s a player. The guys like Jaxson, Joe [Flacco], Lamar [Jackson], they all understand that so well. That’s why the players love them so much. But the other side of the coin is he’s the quarterback. He’s got to know the most. He’s got to do the most. He has the most impact probably on the game of anybody. So, that part of it is just kind of understood. But those guys, man, they’ve been doing it their whole life. They embrace it. NFC East roundtable: Eagles, Cowboys, Commanders enter critical seasons; Giants seek new culture | The Athletic Who’s the player not enough people are talking about who’s going to make a big impact for the team you cover? Carroll: Isaiah Likely was one of the Giants’ biggest free-agent acquisitions, as the tight end signed a three-year, $40 million deal. That type of deal doesn’t usually lead to a player not being talked about enough. However, in a New York media market adoring the Odell Beckham Jr. reunion, while at the same time fixating on Malik Nabers’ return from a torn ACL, Likely has quietly been putting in the work becoming quarterback Jaxson Dart’s go-to pass catcher. As my colleague Dan Duggan noted, Likely was Dart’s favorite target this summer with 44 catches in 11-on-11 team periods during camp. With or without Nabers’ return in Week 1, Likely figures to be a big piece of this offense. After years of losing, Giants star says, ‘My urgency level is high. This doesn’t last forever’ | NJ.com Given how small an NFL player’s career window typically winds up being, how eager is Burns to win? “Oh, I’ve been at that point…I don’t really give a f— about surprising nobody,” he said. “I’m just focused on our team, our opponents and get a dub as many times as we can throughout the season — and getting to the big dance. Surprising people and putting the world on notice? I don’t give a f— about none of that. Not anymore. “I used to want to prove people wrong and prove this and prove that. But I got to a point where it’s like now, bro, people are going to say something regardless of whether you’re good or whether you’re bad. So it really doesn’t matter. The only thing that matters is the work that’s in front of you. I’m not doing this to prove to nobody else. I do it more so to prove to my guys and myself that we can win.” Giants hope new D-coordinator will be one to finally stop Dak Prescott | New York Post The next coordinator in line is Dennard Wilson, who will be making his Giants debut Sunday and he doesn’t care about Giants-Cowboys history. “We’re going to be unapologetic on how we play,” he said. “We’re going to be decisive in what we do. We’re going to play with an edge. We’re going to play with toughness. We’re going to bring violence. That’s our M.O. That’s how the guys have been going out — doing their work every day, their daily business. And that’s how we’re going to play.” NFL Week 1 picks, predictions, schedule, odds, fantasy tips | ESPN.com What we’re hearing on the Giants: It’s the first game of the John Harbaugh era. It’s QB Jaxson Dart’s first opening game start in the NFL. The Giants say they believe they have their signal-caller and coach and that it will lead to wins. Immediately. “I want to do something special. And all the guys in the locker room are, too. We’re starving for this,” Dart said. Bold prediction: Giants rookie WR Malachi Fields will lead the team in receiving yards. It remains to be seen exactly how close to 100% Malik Nabers (knee) is. Fields had a great camp and the Cowboys CBs DaRon Bland and Cobie Durant are beatable. Kurt Warner on being benched for Eli Kurt Warner offers some fascinating insight into why Tom Coughlin turned to Eli Manning. Hearing it from this perspective really puts into context the importance of recognizing an opportunity and capitalizing when the championship window is open. Very well said @kurt13warner 🫡 pic.twitter.com/Yf8xQlDVVF — ΛWTHΞИƬIK (@awthentik) September 9, 2026 Lawrence Taylor Leads Six Giants Named to Sporting News’ 140 Greatest Players Ever | SI.com Taylor ranked fourth on Iyer’s list, going down as the greatest defensive player in league history. The only other defensive players included in the top ten were Reggie White (5th) and Aaron Donald (8th). Only Jim Brown, Jerry Rice, and Tom Brady ranked ahead of Taylor. Michael Strahan is the most recent Giants player to make Iyer’s list. The NFL’s sixth-leading sack-getter ranked 81st. Most of the Giants players included came long before the modern era of the NFL. Mel Hein, who played for Big Blue from 1931 to 1945, was the earliest player to make the cut, ranking 90th. Hein played both center and linebacker and remains the only offensive lineman in NFL history to win MVP. Linebacker Sam Huff (ranked 136th), offensive tackle Roosevelt Brown (98th), and safety Emlen Tunnell (76th) all played together for the Giants in the 1950s, winning a championship in 1956. Each player is a member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame. From Big Blue View Can revamped Giants defense handle high-powered Dallas offense? Nabers, working his way back from a Week 4 torn ACL last season, was a full practice participant all three days this week. No other Giant carries an injury designation heading into the game. For the Cowboys, running back Malik Davis (hip) is out. Nabers had said Thursday that the Giants were leaving the decision up to him. “It’s my career and it’s my body,” Nabers said. “The decision is the decision. title: NY Giants-Cowboys matchup: Can revamped New York defense handle Dallas?
summary: The New York Giants open the season on Sunday Night Football at MetLife Stadium against Dak Prescott and the Dallas Cowboys. The Cowboys are favored by three points, and the Over/Under is set at 48.5 points. The start of the 2026 NFL season is here! Prescott and Dallas have controlled the Giants for the better […]
full_text: Brian Burns (0) | Brad Penner-Imagn Images The New York Giants open the season on Sunday Night Football at MetLife Stadium against Dak Prescott and the Dallas Cowboys. The Cowboys are favored by three points, and the Over/Under is set at 48.5 points. The start of the 2026 NFL season is here! Prescott and Dallas have controlled the Giants for the better half of a decade; Prescott is 14-3 against the Giants with 4,346 passing yards, 31 touchdowns, just nine interceptions, and an impressive 101.5 passer rating. Dallas had a 13-game winning streak over the Giants before their Week 18 loss last season ( 34-17 ) where Prescott and the Dallas’ starters played just the first half. However, John Harbaugh and his distinguished résumé are looking to change the fortunes of the Giants, and they’ll have an excellent opportunity to do so in Week 1, with the entire NFL world watching. Both Dallas and New York fired their defensive coordinators and added key defensive personnel, which should make for some physical football. Dennard Wilson and the Giants defense should have their work cut out for them, even with the injury to Dallas’ starting offensive lineman, Tyler Smith, who underwent thumb surgery on Tuesday and is expected to miss four-to-six weeks. The injury places T.J. Bass as the starter next to Tyler Guyton ( LT ) and center Cooper Beebe. The matchup Smith’s injury is a tough loss for Dallas, but it presents an excellent opportunity for Wilson and the Giants’ defense to manipulate and attack the Cowboys’ protection while weakening a rushing attack led by the newly paid Javonte Williams, who signed a three-year, $24 million deal during the offseason. The loss of Dexter Lawrence is good news for Dallas, but competent veteran depth like D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris is no slouch. Brian Schottenheimer will likely still attempt to establish the run on the road; Dallas averaged 4.8 yards per carry in their two matchups against New York last season, with a total of 58 carries. New York MUST prove able to stop the run on early downs, which will force the Cowboys into longer third-down situations, where we can see Wilson dive into his bag of tricks. I expect to see manipulation from Wilson in passing situations — similar to what we saw under Wink Martindale: wasted blockers, unorthodox pressure via simulated/creepers, and a lot of slanting/twists up front. The middle of the field upgrades with Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese provide tighter windows against the Cowboys’ efficient quick game, which could lead to trap situations with robber coverage from Jevon Holland, Tyler Nubin, or Ar’Darius Washington. Dallas will likely try to quell the potential pressure with play-action bootlegs and easy quick-game options to the flat of 3×1 sets, avoiding the middle of the field early except off back-side reads. I expect a heavy dose of CeeDee Lamb in the quick game, and there will be multiple shots to George Pickens in one-on-one situations against any of the Giants’ cornerbacks. Easing the Cowboys’ offensive line into comfort and slowing down the rush of Abdul Carter, Brian Burns, Kayvon Thibodeaux, and the rest of the Giants can be done by metriculating the ball downfield and putting points on the board; this will be more easily achieved if Dallas can be efficient and successful on early downs. The Giants must be sound in their gap responsibilities against the run, and fast to tackle off the quick-game passing attack — no yards after the catch! Also, of course, tight in their match-principles against Lamb and Pickens. As the game wears on in zone coverage, deeper depth over the middle of the field to eliminate post/dig routes from the dynamic receiving duo. New York must be unpredictable with their pressure decisions, because Prescott is a mastermind at diagnosing and finding answers, but the Giants should incorporate the second level into their four-man pressure packages, specifically targeting Bass. Schottenheimer has the advantage of stressing the Giants’ defense by aligning Lamb and Pickens in a variety of different locations, which will either create mismatches or dictate certain coverages for Wilson and the Giants. The discipline of the cornerback room will be crucial in this matchup. Final thoughts New York does have a fighter’s chance, and they’re only three-point home dogs against a Cowboys team that has dominated them in recent memory. The Giants can win this football game if they slow down Javonte Williams and win some of their one-on-one matchups on the outside. New York needs to win up front in obvious passing situations, and harassing Dak Prescott is an easy — yet difficult to achieve — way to earn a divisional win in John Harbaugh’s first regular-season game as Giants’ coach. Winning will be no cakewalk, but we’ll learn a lot about the Harbaugh-led Giants in Week 1 against the Cowboys.
author: Nick Falato

title: NFL Week 1 picks, predictions: BBV staff split on Giants-Cowboys outcome
summary: Can the New York Giants go against history and upset the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday night? Below, find the Big Blue View staff predictions for that and the rest of the remaining Week 1 slate of NFL games. Chris Pflum Bottom line up front: I’m picking the Giants here. I also have no clue exactly […]
full_text: Can the New York Giants go against history and upset the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday night? Below, find the Big Blue View staff predictions for that and the rest of the remaining Week 1 slate of NFL games. Chris Pflum Bottom line up front: I’m picking the Giants here. I also have no clue exactly how this game is going to play out. There are a ton of unknowns on both sides of the ball. We don’t know exactly what the Cowboys’ defense will look like, and we don’t know what the Giants’ offense or defense will look like between roster and coaching turnover. A year ago I believed that the Giants’ roster was about to hit a critical mass of talent that would allow them to compete week in, week out, without needing to out-scheme their opponents or rely on lucky breaks to win. The results weren’t there, but I do believe the overall talent on the roster put the Giants in position to win more often than not. What I didn’t count on was a lack of accountability and attention to detail from the top down with the Giants’ coaches. This year, I believe the roster is stronger given the continued development of the 2024 and 2025 classes. Ultimately, given all the unknowns in this game, I have to think it will come down to which squad is better prepared for Week 1. And while the Giants’ veteran coaching staff is barely mentioned at the national level, I think they’ve been methodical in how they’ve approached the start of the season. I’m going to trust their experience and clear vision to have the team ready to go on Sunday night. I have no doubts that this is going to be a tough, hard-fought match-up. But I’m going with the Giants starting the season with a statement. Pick: Giants Tony DelGenio 22 years ago, the Giants played their first game under a new, no-nonsense head coach who had almost gotten his team to the Super Bowl a few years earlier. The Giants took a 7-0 lead against the division rival Eagles, but three Donovan McNabb TD passes to Terrell Owens later, Philadelphia won going away. Things eventually worked out, but not in Tom Coughlin’s first season. I expect something similar to happen Sunday, because I feel that the Giants match up poorly with Dallas. The John Harbaugh Giants want to establish the run, but with Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark inside and Rashan Gary outside, that won’t be easy, and the Giants’ middle of the OL is its weakest part at least until rookie Sisi Mauigoa establishes himself. It is also the place from which I expect the Cowboys to generate the most pressure on Jaxson Dart. Dart in principle should be able to do more business through the air, but that depends on his ability to read Dallas’ disguised coverages and whether a thin receiving corps with a lot of question marks can get open and hold onto the ball often enough. On defense I expect more from this Giants team than last year’s. Dennard Wilson’s defense has to be more effective than Shane Bowen’s was. The Cowboys’ offensive line is missing Pro Bowl guard Tyler Smith, and with the Giants’ revamped linebacking corps I expect Dallas’ running game not to be the weapon against the Giants that it has been in the past, even though we haven’t yet seen D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris in Giants blue. My real concern is the secondary. CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens feasted on Giants’ defensive backs last year. We have absolutely no idea how this year’s group, with reclamation projects Deonte Banks and Greg Newsome starting, will fare. And the underrated Dak Prescott always feasts on the Giants’ D and has fun doing it. Coughlin started his Giants career 6-10 in 2004. I expect something similar from Harbaugh, say 7-10, with the first two losses sadly being in Weeks 1 and 2. Pick: Dallas James Hickey The Giants start the 2026 season seeking to replicate a formula that is in many ways the DNA for that has won them four Super Bowls: a defense who success is based on rushing the quarterback and a physical offense with a quarterback who has a knack for making the plays when needed. When it comes to the Giants defense matching up against the Dallas offense it comes down can Brian Burns, Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux get to the quarterback against a banged up Cowboys offense line. Because if given time, Dak Prescott will undoubtedly pick apart a secondary that is starting Tae Banks Week 1. To slow down the Dallas offense, the Giants will need to control the clock with their running game. That brings into the spotlight John Michael Schmitz, the third-year center who has not developed into a top center as hoped. Schmitz will be facing the best defensive tackle tandem in the NFL— Kenny Clark and Quinnen Williams. Since 2016, the four Giants head coaches have split their first games coaching— Ben McAdoo in 2016 Won his debut, 20–19 over the Cowboys and Brian Daboll lead the team to victory in over the Titans in 2020 by a score of 21–20 as Randy Bullock’s 47 yard field goal was wide left as time expired. Pat Shurmur (2018) and Joe Judge (2020) both lost in their debuts. John Harbaugh is not a first-time head coach and will have his team ready for the national Sunday night game. We will see if Dennard Wilson brings an aggressive defense that brings out the best of the players and if the offensive coaching staff can help Jaxson Dart take that proverbial next step. I believe the talent is there and will shine this Sunday. Pick: Giants 27, Dallas 21 David Hartman I’m really torn this week. My heart says a new era is here, and the Giants will turn the page and prevail at home, but my brain says take the Cowboys, who’ve dominated Big Blue for a decade and are coming in with a more proven roster and less change from last season. Like everyone else, I’m really curious to see Harbaugh’s G-Men in action, and excited to see Jaxson Dart, Malik Nabers, and Cam Skattebo on the field together, which we only got for one half of one game last season. Week 1 is always tricky, as we haven’t seen anyone play a meaningful game yet. Can the Giants, minus Dexter Lawrence but plus Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese, plug up a leaky run defense that allowed around 145 rushing yards per game last season (second worst in the NFL)? Can the Cowboys, plus Caleb Downs, fix a pass defense that was easily the worst in the NFL in 2025? In the end, the recent history is too much for me to ignore. The Giants snapped a 9 game losing streak to Dallas when they beat them in Week 18 last season, but that was a meaningless game and Dallas pulled a bunch of their starters early. Even with that game, Dallas has won 16 of the last 18 games between these teams. Pick: Dallas, mostly because taking the Giants would feel to me like Charlie Brown running up to kick the football, and until that ball doesn’t get pulled away, I’m not quite ready to believe. Valentine’s View As many years as I have been covering the Giants, and making predictions about them, I should know better. I do know better. I should make the Giants prove they can win games before I pick them to do that. But, while Mrs. Big Blue View would probably disagree, I prefer to be optimistic. I always want to believe that things are going to turn around for the Giants, that things will get better. When I reflect, I can see why things went sideways under Ben McAdoo, Pat Shurmur, Joe Judge, and Brian Daboll. All of them were trying to learn how to be head coaches, and ultimately proved they weren’t cut from the right cloth. John Harbaugh is different. He has already been there and done that. He doesn’t have to prove his head-coaching credentials to anyone. Harbaugh has brought something different to the Giants. He has raised the expectation for everyone — players, front office, the maintenance guys who put together the players’ temporary locker room quarters. To be honest, maybe even the media covering the team. I am going to believe that the last few months of the entire organization going to Harbaugh University will pay off on Sunday night. Pick: Giants
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants’ OC Matt Nagy will call plays from upstairs vs. Cowboys
summary: After experimenting during the preseason with calling plays from the sideline and upstairs in a booth high above the field, New York Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said Thursday he will work from upstairs Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys. “I’m excited about it. I think that I’ve always been down on the field. When […]
full_text: Matt Nagy | Getty Images After experimenting during the preseason with calling plays from the sideline and upstairs in a booth high above the field, New York Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said Thursday he will work from upstairs Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys. “I’m excited about it. I think that I’ve always been down on the field. When I was a quality control coach, I was up in the box for one year,” Nagy said on Thursday. “So, I wanted to experiment with that in the preseason, and I was able to do that. I really liked it. You can see a lot more from up there.” The tradeoff, of course, is giving up the personal interactions and feeling the game from the sideline. “It takes away a little bit of the on the field element of being able to communicate and talk all the time, but there’s a calm in the box,” Nagy said. “And for me, first time in this role as a play caller, OC being up in that box, I just feel like I can see things a lot better and then have the ultimate trust in the staff and being able to see things so that they can communicate to me what they’re seeing. And we’ve got the telephone, too, so I can always jump on the phone with (quarterback) Jaxson (Dart) if I need to. But I’m excited about that opportunity.” Here are more takeaways from Nagy’s Thursday media availability. On the Giants’ offensive scheme … “What I would say to that is, we talk about, Coach Harbs (Head Coach John Harbaugh) talks about principles and methods and what that means and you can relay that to an offense is, I learned this game through Andy Reid, (former NFL coach) Marty Morningweg when I was in Philadelphia. And I learned that foundation of this offense and that offense for me. Took it to Kansas City, took it to Chicago, and now here I am. And again, this opportunity that I have is a first for me. So, being here to be able to take some of the things that we do as a staff and make it ours, that’s been some of the times for me selfishly, it’s been fun just putting this thing together. So, I’m excited to see how this thing goes this year, because I think you’re going to see it’s our offense. It’s no other offense from prior history. You know, it’s ours.” On what he wants to see from Jaxson Dart … “We want Jaxson to be able to play fast. We want him to be himself. He’s a special talent. And it’s our job as coaches to take all this time that we’ve had to do it. And that’s what we’ve put together is a game plan that we think is to his strengths. But at the same point in time too, we got to make sure that there’s going to be times in the game where we just got to let him cut it loose and continue to build every week. This isn’t, there’s going to be good plays, there’s going to be bad plays, but how does he keep that up? It’s going to be an emotional time. Sunday night football against the Cowboys, a lot of emotions going on. He’s a competitor. So, I want him to stay calm, extremely confident, play fast and execute and just be a complete leader, but also just be himself, man. Cut it loose and have fun.” On where Dart has grown … “Probably just the confidence and understanding of the concepts that we’re doing, both run and pass. There was probably some frustration early on because sometimes you don’t know, it’s the first time you’re running a play, you don’t really know the play. And now when we’re out here, he knows the play, he has multiple reps. And so, we can build off of that. We can teach off of that. Now we’ve got to transfer it to the game and some unscouted looks. And so, I think for him, again, his growth, and he’s so mature for being 23 years old and having limited experience in the NFL, super mature, very calm, but he’s really good. So, we got to make sure we use his strengths.” On Odell Beckham’s acceptance of his role … “He hasn’t brought that up at all as far as that part of it, which is probably hard. Odell has come to me at times and we’ve had some good conversations where he’ll almost come to me like I’m the conduit between him and Jaxson because he wants to be careful and gentle with how much he gets in Jaxson’s ear, with how he, he’s played a lot of football. He’s seen a lot of things. And so, what I can do is I can balance some of the questions he has and filter it to Jaxson. And then the other times he goes to Jaxson. But what I find really professional about Odell is that he doesn’t want to put too much on Jaxson’s plate mentally. And I think he’s in a good spot too. You guys see what he can do. He can do a lot of good things, but we also have a lot in this offense and there’s details. So, every now and then, if he screws up an assignment, the biggest thing we say is don’t do it again. And he’s done a good job with that.”
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants’ rookie placekicker, long-snapper have earned the team’s trust
summary: When John Harbaugh was hired as New York Giants’ head coach, it figured that a makeover of the kicking game would follow. Harbaugh, after all, is a former special teams coach who has always emphasized that part of the game. The Giants’ kicking game in recent seasons has been lackluster. The Giants made Jordan Stout […]
full_text: Jordan Stout (15) and Dominic Zvada (34) watch a field goal sail through the uprights. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect When John Harbaugh was hired as New York Giants’ head coach, it figured that a makeover of the kicking game would follow. Harbaugh, after all, is a former special teams coach who has always emphasized that part of the game. The Giants’ kicking game in recent seasons has been lackluster. The Giants made Jordan Stout the game’s highest-paid punter, bringing one of the best in the league at that job from the Baltimore Ravens, Harbaugh’s former employer. No surprise there. The other two kicking-game specialist roles belong to undrafted, with Dominic Zvada as the placekicker and Ben Mann as the long-snapper. That could be considered a surprise. Zvada won a competition with veteran Jason Sanders, who was released during the spring, and Ben Sauls, who was went 8 of 8 as the Giants’ placekicker at the end of last season. After Casey Kreiter left for the Arizona Cardinals in free agency, the Giants signed Mann and journeyman Zach Triner. They quickly released Triner in the spring, and never brought in other competition for Mann. Zvada appreciates Harbaugh’s trust. “There’s a certain level of trust that he [Harbaugh] has,” Zvada said recently in the Giants’ locker room. “Obviously, bringing in two rookies, that’s how you have to go at it. But it also shows, at least from what I see, his knowledge of specialists. “Ben’s done a great job. I think I’ve done a really good job. Obviously, Jordan’s been doing a really good job for the last few years. So, he seems confident in who he wants to bring in. I think we’re a great group, and we’re going to do really good this year.” Zvada and Mann will be roommates this season. Mann said he finds it “amazing” that he gets to partner with Zvada. “I’ve definitely thought about it, and I’m just so grateful for the opportunity because I definitely do think about it,” Mann said. “I think it’s amazing. There’s only so many rookies that start every year at these two positions, and for us to be here together is obviously a great thing. For the coaches to be putting that much trust in the players we are now and the players we’ll develop into really means a ton.” Zvada added that it is “kind of nice going through it with somebody who’s in the same situation. I talked to some other guys around the league that were in my class. And they don’t have this sort of thing. So, it’s very nice to have this.” Stout, a 2025 All-Pro who is in his fifth NFL season, revealed that Harbaugh and special teams coach Chris Horton, who had that role for 12 years in Baltimore, sought his input when sifting through placekicking and snapping specialists. “Chris and Harbaugh were both extremely diligent with finding the right person,” Stout said. “They were talking to me through the whole process, asking me to look at specific guys and who do you like, who do you not like? “Chris and Harbs have been with the best in the world. They’ve been with [placekicker] Justin Tucker, they’ve been with [long-snapper] Nick Moore, who’s an incredible long snapper. They had [punter] Sam Koch in Baltimore for 16 years. I mean, they know what greatness looks like. These guys, they were the best out there and they are really, really talented and it’s gonna be a lot of fun to play with them.” Zvada ‘thankful’ for opportunity Coming off a season at Michigan that was not the best of his four-year college career, Zvada just wanted a chance. “Really, all I wanted was an opportunity and Coach Harbaugh gave me that opportunity,” Zvada said. “I was able to show up and do what I wanted to do, or do what I needed to do. Be able to prove myself and Coach Harbaugh gave me that opportunity. So, I was really thankful for that. It’s worked out so far and I’m going to keep going with it.“ Zvada, 22, had two exceptional collegiate seasons, and two so-so seasons. He said his focus is “just getting better at being consistent.” “I mean, for me, it’s all focused on this season,” Zvada said. “I think. I’ve done a good job so far and I think at the beginning of every year I want to lay out a plan of how I want to attack each part of the year. And so far, where I’m at, I’m very happy with how things have gone so far. “It’s all about staying consistent. It’s all about going into the season with the momentum, having a good preseason, having a good camp, those sort of things. And those things start with having good momentum during the summer. So, it all kind of ties together.” Horton said Zvada achieved the consistency he was looking for. “Dom just showed consistency from the day he walked in,” Horton said. “There’s just been a lot of consistency, and going out there, and kicks being made, right? We started with the process. Again, we broke down everything, how he kicked, how he wanted the ball. We talked to (punter) Jordan (Stout) a lot about, like, let’s fine-tune these things to help him, to give him the best chance. Really, to give both guys the best opportunity, but since he’s walked in this building, he’s been very consistent.” The swirling winds of the Meadowlands have given many placekickers fits. Zvada is confident he can figure them out. “I played in the Big Ten. I don’t know how it is here, but I’ve played in elements before,” Zvada said. “Certainly, the practice field here in the Meadowlands is windy. “For me, you know, it’s the same sort of thing with the yardages. I would go out there and I’d pretend the wind’s not even there. Unless it’s a side wind, then you’ve got to play it. But, I’m going to hit it the same way.” Zvada made a handful of kicks beyon 60 yards during training camp. So, what is his range? “I’ll say deep,” Zvada said. “That’s all I’ll say.” Mann: ‘A complete dream come true’ No matter who else called, Mann was not saying no when an offer came from the Giants. “Playing for the Giants is a complete dream come true,” Mann said. “Growing up in the Northeast, starting in Pennsylvania, going to school in Connecticut and then Boston .. it’s a team I kind of grew up rooting for. “My grandfather [Chuck Mercein] was drafted here a long, long time ago. And if you told me I’d have an offer from all 32 teams, I think the Giants are the team I would choose. With everything that’s going on here, the opportunities, on and off the field, the new coaching staff, everything, there’s so many factors that would draw me to this team.” Mann did not intend to make long-snapping a career. He was a tight end and defensive end in high school, as well a lacrosse and basketball player. He went to Yale to play tight end, with snapping as a secondary skill. Mann and his coaches quickly realized he was a better snapper than tight end, and soon enough that was all he was doing. “It was funny, it was definitely a transition for me. Because when I first got to Yale, I committed, at least in my mind, as a tight end that kind of did long snapping on the side,” Mann said. “And I quickly found out I was better than I realized at long snapping. “And once I was a starting long snapper, they took away my role as a tight end. And I wasn’t really practicing as much. I was standing on the sidelines doing my snaps, not playing scout offense. And it drove me wild for a while, because I went from a three-sport athlete, came in what I thought was a tight end, and then I kind of got, I fell into my role as a long snapper. And I was just out there restless.” While it took time to accept and adjust to his new reality, Mann has ended up “grateful” for the decision. “I definitely went back and forth with my coach about it, but I always knew they were doing what was best for me and what was best for the team,” Mann said. “And it drove me nuts, but they were right. “So, I always thank them and I’m grateful for them.” Mann finished his collegiate career at Boston College in 2025, and then landed with the Giants. summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know on a day we remember those that we lost 25 years ago today. full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know on a day we remember those that we lost 25 years ago today. Big things expected from John Harbaugh’s Giants | ESPN.com This is Harbaugh’s program. He’s hoping building a bigger, more physical team pays immediate dividends because the schedule doesn’t let Harbaugh’s Giants ease into the flow. The Giants face an unusually big game in Week 1 considering they get the Super Bowl favorite Los Angeles Rams on the road next Monday night. It makes their matchup in Week 1 with a division rival that has owned them for years that much more critical. But nobody seems to be giving Harbaugh the sort of grace period new head coaches generally receive. Instead, the rhetoric is to turn it around immediately, even though the Giants won seven games combined the past two seasons. “I get it from the standpoint of expectations, but of course we expect to win,” Harbaugh said. “How do you go out there and compete at this level if you don’t expect to win? If you don’t expect to win, you certainly aren’t going to. I’ve said this before, we expect and we plan to and we’ll be playing to win every single one of our games this year. That’s our expectation, that’s our plan, that’s what we’ll be striving for. We think we can [win], we believe we can [win], wholeheartedly.” Giants-Dallas is a hot ticket Think Giants fans are excited for their first game with John Harbaugh as head coach? The current get-in price for Sunday night vs. the Cowboys at @TickPick is $242 and the average purchase price is $369, the highest ever at MetLife in TickPick’s history (since 2011). #Partner pic.twitter.com/MDYnJMhtyI — Field Yates (@FieldYates) September 10, 2026 2026 NFL offensive line rankings: Broncos, Eagles and Buccaneers open in top three | PFF 23. New York Giants. Andrew Thomas was arguably the Giants’ best player last year, as his 90.3 PFF grade tied for a career high. His issue has been staying healthy, having missed significant time both in 2023 and 2024. New York drafted Francis Mauigoa in the first round, and if he can hit the ground running, then the unit looks a lot stronger. But, it’s a group that just might be another season away from making a bigger impact. How Giants are molding Jaxson Dart into savior they need him to be | The Athletic Harbaugh oversaw one of the best Year 2 leaps in NFL history while in Baltimore. After making seven starts as a raw rookie in 2018, Lamar Jackson blossomed into an MVP while leading the Ravens to an NFL-best 14-2 record in his second season. No one is banking on that type of breakout season for Dart. But there is at least a blueprint for the coaching staff to follow as Dart transitions into his second season. “I think the approach has been similar from the basic idea that we’re trying to build an offense for Jaxson Dart that is amenable to his skill set,” Harbaugh said. “We did the same thing with Lamar. But they’re different people, different quarterbacks — all those kinds of things are different.” Unexpected Match: John Harbaugh & Jaxson Dart’s Obsession Could Be Enough To Fix Giants | FOX Sports On paper, it’s a mismatch. The 63-year-old coach with a somewhat stoic, all-football demeanor and the flashy 23-year-old who seems to love everything that comes with being a celebrity in New York. Dart is a showman, whether it’s on Instagram, at parties or on celebrity row. Harbaugh, on the other hand, seems more at home in a film room with the lights down low. But what Harbaugh quickly learned was that Dart’s appearance was deceiving. The old coach spent hours talking with the young quarterback before he took the Giants job. That’s where he first learned of Dart’s “obsession” with the details, with becoming a better quarterback, and with the hard work he knew he had to put in to get there. And just in case he wasn’t convinced, he took calls from former Giants coach Brian Daboll, Eli Manning, and several others raving about Dart’s football acumen and work ethic, too. Jaxson Dart’s 10-word text to Giants linemen reveals QB’s bold intentions before facing Cowboys | New York Post The text was sent Tuesday night. Late. “It was kind of just random, out of nowhere,’’ left guard Jon Runyan Jr. told The Post. Jaxson Dart has several different text chains within the Giants locker room, and this particular one was with the five starting offensive linemen. The message was transmitted into the phones of Runyan, Andrew Thomas, John Michael Schmitz Jr., Francis Mauigoa and Jermaine Eluemunor. Giants’ Darius Slayton replacement ready for big shot vs. Cowboys: ‘Pressure is a privilege’ | NJ.com John Harbaugh, the Giants’ new coach and football czar, sent Darius Slayton packing because he believes he has better options to play opposite Malik Nabers. And those two outside receiver options — who both now face significant pressure — are seventh-year pro Darnell Mooney and intriguing third-round rookie Malachi Fields, a big-bodied red-zone weapon. So what does Fields think about being thrust into a significant role immediately, starting with Sunday night’s enormous season opener at home against Dallas? OBJ’s Blonde debut (h/t Art Stapleton) Old school Odell pic.twitter.com/5u5cI9ybdv — Art Stapleton (@art_stapleton) September 10, 2026 Why New York Giants are taking different approach to team captains in 2026 | USAToday.com Game-day captains were handled differently. Rather than naming a permanent group for the season, Harbaugh selected captains on a week-to-week basis. The choices could change depending on circumstances, the opponent, or simply an opportunity to recognize a particular player’s leadership. Rather than relying solely on traditional captains, they have established a leadership council selected by their teammates consisting of Andrew Thomas, Jaxson Dart, Jevon Holland, Jordan Stout, Brian Burns, Jameis Winston, Tremaine Edmunds and Chris Manhertz. Outside the gates of the stadium, The Tunnel to Towers Foundation will conclude their Steel Across America tour with an authentic steel beam from the World Trade Center displayed, creating a visible reminder of the resilience and unity that emerged in the aftermath of 9/11. Players and coaches from both teams will also wear commemorative NYPD, FDNY and PAPD pregame apparel, along with “Never Forget” t-shirts. A limited number of hats will be available in the team store on gameday, with proceeds benefiting the respective first responder agencies. Fans are encouraged to be in their seats by 8pm for player introductions, when the Giants will take the field led by New York City first responders, who will form a gauntlet for the team to run through. title: Jets vs Titans: Predictions for the season opener
summary: The New York Jets go on the road to Nashville, Tennessee as they face the Tennessee Titans on Sunday to open their 2026 campaign. The Titans, as everybody will remind you this week, hired former Jets head coach Robert Saleh as their new head coach this offseason. That makes this a so-called “revenge game” for […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 14: Braelon Allen #0 of the New York Jets celebrates his first-quarter touchdown with teammates against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at MetLife Stadium on August 14, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New York Jets go on the road to Nashville, Tennessee as they face the Tennessee Titans on Sunday to open their 2026 campaign. The Titans, as everybody will remind you this week, hired former Jets head coach Robert Saleh as their new head coach this offseason. That makes this a so-called “revenge game” for Saleh and the Titans, though in general I think the revenge angle is overrated in these games. The Jets and the Titans both finished the 2025 season with a 3-14 record. This is not exactly must see TV for the average NFL fan. Both teams are looking to get off to a good start in 2026, and both fanbases view the opposing team as one of the games their team should win this season. Barring a tie, one team and their fans will go home disappointed and worried about “sheesh, if we are losing to the lowly [Jets/Titans] this is going to be a long season.” While it may well be a long season for one or both teams, I don’t think this is a so-called must win game for either team. Aside from the inherent absurdity of labeling any one game at the beginning of the season a must win game, it probably makes sense to note that opening day has become increasingly unpredictable as NFL teams refuse to play their starters in the preseason. Many teams look completely unprepared on opening day, and surprising results abound. If the Jets win, great! If they don’t, I don’t think that means the season is a lost cause. Let’s make a few predictions for the game on Sunday. The Jets revamped run defense starts the season with a bang, holding Titans running backs to less than 8o combined yards on the ground. The Jets have brought in a bunch of run stuffers this offseason, and the Titans offensive line is less than ideal. Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears may find little space to run against the Jets thumpers. The Jets pass defense struggles as Cam Ward feeds Wandale Robinson, Tyjae Spears, Gunnar Helm and Carnell Tate against a suspect Jets secondary and linebackers. Ward was bad last year in his rookie season, but he ended the season on an up note. Over his last four complete games Ward threw eight touchdown passes and just one interception. In addition, Ward faced the toughest group of pass defenses of any quarterback in the NFL last season. The Jets are not a tough pass defense. Ward will take advantage. The Jets will struggle to get off the field on third down and Ward will throw for 250+ passing yards and two touchdowns. Former Jets pass rushers Jermaine Johnson and John Franklin Myers will get stonewalled most of the night by the Jets bookend tackles. They will combine for less than one sack. Jeffrey Simmons and the Titans interior linemen will, however, feast against the less sturdy interior of the Jets offensive line, combining for 2+ sacks. Geno Smith will throw for 250+ yards and two touchdowns, as the expected defensive struggle instead turns into a bit of a surprising shootout between Ward and Smith. Both quarterbacks take advantage of suspect secondaries. Breece Hall puts up 100+ yards from scrimmage and the Jets running backs run for 120+ rushing yards combined against a Titans run defense hurting from the loss of linebacker Cedric Gray to a concussion. Braelon Allen runs one in for a touchdown as the Jets take the opener, 27 – 20. These predictions are just for fun. Betting based on some random dude on the internet having some fun would be very poor judgment and can be hazardous to your financial health. If you choose to bet on the game make your own calls. You can head over to our friends at FanDuel Sportsbook for all your gambling needs.

title: Three things I’m looking at in the Jets vs Titans Game
summary: It’s an honor to be featured on Gang Green Nation, and I can’t wait to talk Jets football with you all season! In a world full of emotional recollections and irrational takes, I aim to be the purveyor of truth for this passionate fan base. While I wholeheartedly root for the team day in and […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TN - SEPTEMBER 29: Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets is hit while throwing a pass by Jurrell Casey #99 of the Tennessee Titans at LP Field on September 29, 2013 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Wesley Hitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s an honor to be featured on Gang Green Nation, and I can’t wait to talk Jets football with you all season! In a world full of emotional recollections and irrational takes, I aim to be the purveyor of truth for this passionate fan base. While I wholeheartedly root for the team day in and day out and yearn for the day they can reward me as my Knicks have, my pieces are grounded in logic, reason, and provable data. I’m going to use those three principles to assess the three things I discuss in this article about the Jets/Titans game. Of course, there are plenty of obvious storylines here (revenge game, anyone!?), but two things I will guarantee in my weekly previews are that I will never just echo the mainstream narrative, and you will always learn at least one new stat you’ve never seen before. The mainstream narrative here is revenge, and that’s fair. This is more than Robert Saleh looking to spite the owner who fired him mid-season; it is more than Aaron Glenn trying to prove Woody was right to choose him instead of sticking with Saleh. A whopping 20.7% of the total players rostered in this game are preparing to face either their old team or old coach this Sunday. The revenge angle will be heavily prevalent throughout the game, but let’s look at things that are more easily measured than vengeance: Geno Smith Under Pressure A lot of the eyes on Geno will be looking to answer the question, “Is this Seahawks Geno or Raiders Geno?” I regret to inform you that they’re the same person. He can put up yards with high usage, and he throws picks with his fearless nature – these things have rung true all four years as a starter in his 30s. Another constant from that entire four-year span is how badly he folds under pressure. Last year in particular, he had the single worst drop in PFF grade when pressured vs clean pocket in the entire NFL. His 79.9 grade dropped all the way down to 28.8 for the 212 dropbacks in which he was pressured. There were several QBs who had their grades drop 40+ when pressured, but Geno was the lone QB in the NFL to drop 50+. Six of his league-leading 17 interceptions came from plays where he was under pressure. The Jets offensive line is coming off a year where they were the only team in the NFL to have exactly one combination of linemen start for all 17 games. They replaced John Simpson with Dylan Parham, extended Joe Tippmann, and seem poised to take another step together as one of football’s younger ascending units. Will this line, Frank Reich’s game-planning, and Geno’s pre-play diagnoses abolish all instances of pressure? Statistics (and common sense) say probably not, as Saleh has consistently been one of the best minds in the sport at this exact skill. In 2023, Saleh’s Jets led the league in Sack %, and they were 2 nd in the league five weeks into 2024 before he was shown the door (they fell outside of the top 5 under Jeff Ulbrich’s watch). Armed with equally motivated ex-Jets Jermaine Johnson II, John Franklin-Myers, and the established Titans All-Pro DT Jeffery Simmons, I’d imagine he’s looking to continue his efficiency in this stat. Perhaps the greatest aspect of Saleh’s defensive scheme is the ability to create pressure without blitzing. They rush with four, have seven in coverage, and make it that much more difficult for opposing QBs to make good decisions. Geno has been struggling so much with pressure vs. teams that actually blitz, meaning there are five or six players in coverage and he’s making the wrong decision. How much will that be amplified if he’s under pressure and there are seven players in coverage? I’m extremely curious to see how much pressure Saleh’s Titans can generate, and even more curious to see how Geno and the Jets respond. Will there be more calamity? Has Frank schemed up some outlet/checkdown options? Can Geno play with poise and make smart decisions? I have my popcorn ready! All Stuffed Up? I don’t especially enjoy Kool-Aid, so I don’t often drink it, but I might be in on the Kool-Aid for T’Vondre Sweat. There just aren’t too many guys his size that move that quickly, and I love the sneak peek we got vs. the Giants in preseason a couple of weeks ago. One of the clearest issues for the Jets last year was the run defense – the Jets allowed the 4th most rushing yards per game on the 10th most yards per carry, and after Quinnen Williams was traded, there was no answer for the opposing running backs. This season, Darren Mougey signed David Onyemata, secured a trade for T’Vondre Sweat, and brought in a desperately needed veteran presence in the linebacker room in Demario Davis. I cannot overstate how impressive it is that 15-year veteran Demario Davis is coming off a season in which he had his career-high in tackles (143). He also had a career-high 16 run stuffs and 6 tackles for loss. The combination of his physical skill set with his football intellect will be perfect for Jamien Sherwood, who was still a tackling machine last year (154) but looked lost at times. With Cam Ward a sophomore QB learning a new system and young, developing weapons, we can say with absolute certainty that Titans OC Brian Daboll will look to run the football. Between Tony Pollard, Tyjae Spears, and Nicholas Singleton, they feel good about their options in the room. Pollard is coming off a 1,082-yard campaign with five touchdowns and 4.5 yards per carry, which are all better than Breece Hall’s 2025 numbers. There’s a lot of attention on a “Cam vs Geno” discussion, but I truly believe that in these first two points, we have established the actual two keys of the game. The Jets will need Geno to survive the inevitable pressure when it comes, and the Titans will need to somehow get Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears consistently running past their former teammate T’Vondre Sweat. The Dark Cloud If you’re a Jets fan, you know about the dubious interception stat that is clouding the Aaron Glenn Jets era. The three-time Pro Bowl cornerback-turned-defensive coordinator-turned-head coach spearheaded the first team in NFL history to record zero interceptions in a full season. Fun fact: seasons used to be 16 games long; they were previously 14 games long, and teams still managed to grab an interception during the season. 17 games, and Aaron Glenn’s team was completely empty-handed. Until they get one, this dark cloud will loom over them. Glenn could fire all the coaches he wants, make all the excuses he needs to feel better, but nothing can erase this embarrassing 2025 record, and until they get one in 2026, the monkey will still be on their back. The good news is that this regime knows this! They signed Nahshon Wright, who tied for second last year in most interceptions (5), Dane Belton, who had a pick last year (and is a tackling machine), drafted star cornerback D’Angelo Ponds, and traded for All-Pro Safety Minkah Fitzpatrick. It should be inarguable that the personnel in the secondary is much more equipped to catch interceptions than last year’s bunch. It should also be noted that the earlier point about Geno Smith throwing picks in duress works for lots of other teams as well. If the Jets can generate pressure much more efficiently than they did last year, then perhaps a young QB (say, like Cam Ward) would panic under pressure and throw it directly to the Jets’ secondary. They made a huge upgrade there by drafting David Bailey second overall and signing Joseph Ossai and Kingsley Enagbare. Ossai’s not healthy, so we can omit him for this Sunday preview, but let’s see what the second overall pick can do in his NFL debut. With Will McDonald IV on the other side, there should be opportunity to get after the quarterback and force mistakes, but I admittedly said the same thing last year with…
