title: NFL players, coaches, execs remember 9/11 on 25th anniversary
summary: Hall of Famers, franchise greats and more recount the moments they experienced in the aftermath of the attacks.
full_text:
Deep sighs. Long pauses. Cracked voices.

 Twenty-five years later, it's still hard for some in the NFL community to talk about the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks -- any community, for that matter. The pain and trauma from the tragedies in New York; Washington, D.C.; and Shanksville, Pennsylvania, will be felt for generations.

 Like the rest of the country, the NFL was reeling in the aftermath. Players, coaches and officials were gripped by grief, fear and confusion -- raw emotions that gradually shifted over the course of 12 tumultuous days.

 

 By the time they resumed games on Sept. 23 -- a hiatus that included intense, behind-the-scenes meetings on when it was appropriate to play football again -- the league had experienced a look-in-the-mirror moment that many believe set up a return that was galvanizing for the nation.

 To commemorate the anniversary, ESPN is sharing the 9/11 experiences of more than a dozen people: Players, coaches, team officials, a league official and a fan who believes his love for the New York Giants saved his life.

 Their memories are vivid. They remember the sense of pride born from the restorative healing process, and they remember the profound sadness.

 Chris Mara, now a top Giants executive and a member of the Mara family that founded the franchise, began his interview with an apology.

 "Please bear with me, this isn't going to be easy. I lost four close friends that day," he said, clearing his throat. "But we'll get through it."

 A quarter-century later, the effects are still felt, but we examine how they got through the trying times -- along with the lasting impact.

 Jump to a section: 
 'All hell broke loose' 
 'Some things I wish I had never seen' 
 'We're not going to play' 
 'There wasn't a dry eye' 
 'The best in people' 

 

 

 

 'All hell broke loose' 
 The NFL was waking up on a Tuesday (the day off for players) when, in the span of 51 minutes on a brilliantly sunny day, three hijacked planes struck the north and south towers of the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. At 10:03 a.m., four minutes after the first of the two towers collapsed, United Flight 93 from Newark, New Jersey, crashed in a field near Shanksville as passengers fought a valiant battle against the hijackers. 

 The New York Jets , based on Long Island at the time, were only 20 miles from the Towers. The Giants, who lost the night before in Denver, arrived at Newark on a red-eye shortly before Flight 93 took off and about 90 minutes before the first tower was hit. Some in their traveling party exited the airport via the United terminal. 

 What follows is an oral history, with accounts from people who were there (titles from 2001). 

 Ernie Accorsi, Giants general manager: We didn't find out until later that the gate next to ours was the terrorist plane, the one that crashed in Pennsylvania. [Giants personnel] walked right by that plane boarding.

 Michael Strahan, Giants player: It kind of messes with your mind because you realize at the time that we were leaving the airport, walking through the terminal, people were going to get on these flights that we all know did not end well.

 Tiki Barber, Giants player: I lived on the Upper East Side of Manhattan when I was playing. I remember getting home, my wife was at work, I was home by myself. You started to hear rumblings from people texting you or calling you. I didn't answer my phone because I wanted to go to sleep. I kept getting these phone calls, phone calls, phone calls, text messages.

 Eventually I answered one and they said, "Turn on your TV, this is crazy. Are you OK?"

 Herm Edwards, Jets coach: I can remember sitting in my office. It was a beautiful day. From my office, you could always see planes going to LaGuardia.

 Around when 9/11 happened, I didn't see any planes. I was like, "That's strange. Why are there no planes in the air?" Usually, you see them. It didn't sound right. It didn't look right. I turned the television on, and when I turned the television on, I saw it. I'm like, "Are you kidding me?"

 Vinny Testaverde, Jets player: A bunch of us were watching it unfold on TV in the trainers' room, and you could see guys getting nervous and talking about what the possibilities were.

 Shortly after that, everyone took off and went home. I remember calling my wife on the way home, telling her to get the kids out of school. We were all nervous, on edge.

 Strahan: I was at home, Montclair, New Jersey, sleeping. Phone rings, pick up the phone and someone says, "Look out the window." And from where I lived, I had a view of the entire Manhattan skyline. I looked out the window, and I saw smoke coming from the first tower.

 Jason Garrett, Giants player: We lived on 79th Street and West End Avenue. ... I think I fell asleep and then I just started hearing these fire trucks going by our window. And it's like sirens and trucks and sirens and trucks. And I'm thinking to myself, "What the hell is going on?"

 Joe Andruzzi, New England Patriots player: I was sitting in a dentist's chair and heard on the radio that a plane hit the towers. So not thinking anything of it, I got back in my car. By then, the second plane had hit and it was all commotion on the radio.

 When I finally realized what the hell was really going on, my heart was in my throat. I just had a gut feeling that one, if not two or three of my brothers [members of the FDNY] were all a part of it.

 Damien Woody, Patriots player: I was in shock at what I was watching, unfolding on television -- an attack on our country, on American soil. That's something I had never seen before. It was surreal, watching everything unfold in real time.

 Accorsi: All hell broke loose. From our practice field [in East Rutherford, New Jersey], you could see the towers smoking.

 Dave Szott, Washington player: I was home in Morristown [New Jersey]. Marty Schottenheimer was the coach and he let me have Monday and Tuesday off with my family. From the hill in my neighborhood, you could see the towers burning. We couldn't get a hold of my brother, Kevin, who was working in Building 5 [at the World Trade Center]. To complicate matters, my brother is visually impaired. He's legally blind. ... So now I have a visually impaired brother we can't get a hold of, possibly involved directly.

 Mara: My daughter, Kate [an actress] was headed to L.A. from New York on an American Airlines flight that left basically when all the other planes that crashed took off. We went through many hours of trying to figure out where she was and was she being affected by this? Were there going to be any more planes that it was going to happen to? We had no idea. It was pretty hairy.

 Barber: I didn't know what to do. I always kind of know what to do. I'm aware, I feel like I can see things, I understand things. I had no idea what to do and I felt lost.

 Kevin Mawae, Jets player: There are people who can tell you exactly where they were when JFK was shot. I know exactly where I was when the Challenger blew up in '86. There are defining moments in people's lives that change the entire world. You remember those things with clarity that's [unbelievable]; 9/11 is the same way.

 Garrett: The world was about to change.

 

 

 

 'Some things I wish I had never seen' 

 More than 3,000 people were killed in the attacks. NFL teams returned to work the following day for practice even though there was uncertainty on whether the Week 2 games would be played. It was a time for reflection. 

 In the ensuing days, the Jets and Giants boarded buses and visited Ground Zero to deliver supplies and boost the morale of rescue workers. The Washington players went to Arlington National Cemetery for a memorial service. Players visited fire departments, police stations and hospitals. 

 Some waited anxiously to hear from loved ones. Everywhere there were chilling reminders of what had occurred. 

 Barber: A sinking feeling came to me when I realized that the Giants Stadium parking lot…

title: NFL Week 1 predictions: Upsets, fantasy sleepers, stat lines
summary: Could DeVonta Smith find the end zone in Week 1? Will the Jets finally intercept a pass? What will Aidan Hutchinson's stat line look like Sunday?
full_text:
The 2026 NFL season is underway, with the Seahawks and 49ers already crowned as winners in Week 1. But what will happen in the remaining 14 games? We have 15 predictions from our NFL experts.

 First, betting analyst Pamela Maldonado picks two underdogs who could win outright, Then, analytics writer Seth Walder projected out stat lines for three players. Fantasy football writer Eric Moody gives three sleepers, and analyst Matt Bowen suggests three players who will find the end zone. Finally, analyst Ben Solak lays out four wild-card predictions.

 Could the Broncos upset the Chiefs? Will Cowboys tight end Jake Ferguson  score a touchdown? And is Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis flying under the fantasy radar? Let's make 15 big predictions for all the action on Sunday and Monday.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Upset picks | Projected stat lines 
 Fantasy sleepers, surprises 
 TD scorers | Wild-card predictions 

 
 

 Maldonado predicts two upsets 
 

 New York Jets +1.5 at Tennessee Titans 

 New York's clearest strength can take advantage of Tennessee's biggest weakness Sunday . The Jets added more playmakers to their pass rush alongside  Will McDonald IV , including No. 2 pick David Bailey , while the Titans' offensive line came in at 26th in Mike Clay's positional group rankings . That pressure could force Titans QB Cam Ward  into fumble risk and the hero-ball mistakes that hurt him last season.

 
 

 

 Denver Broncos +2.5 at Kansas City Chiefs 

 Denver has the strong defense to neutralize a Chiefs offense with real questions. Kansas City has vulnerabilities on the offensive line, quarterback Patrick Mahomes  is returning from major knee surgery , and the Chiefs' passing game was already declining before his injury in Week 15 . Denver's biggest edge on  Monday  night should be making Mahomes uncomfortable and turning this into another tight game between the AFC West foes.

 

 

 Walder predicts three stat lines 
 

 Aidan Hutchinson , Edge, Detroit Lions : 2.0 sacks, 7 pressures, 25% pass rush win rate

 I'm already extremely bullish on Hutchinson, who led my seasonlong sack projections . And he's set up extremely well for a lightning-quick start.

 The Lions are seven-point favorites over the Saints , which means there's a high likelihood New Orleans will be behind and forced into must-pass situations. Quarterback  Tyler Shough took sacks at a high 8.3% rate last season, and Hutchinson should have favorable matchups against left tackle  Kelvin Banks Jr . or right tackle Taliese Fuaga . Both tackles were well below average in pass block win rate last season.

 
 

 Adonai Mitchell , WR, New York Jets : 5 receptions, 84 receiving yards, 1 touchdown

 I have been hyping up Mitchell for a while and strongly believe this is the season when it all comes together. The case for Mitchell is simple: He gets open.

 Over the past two seasons combined, Mitchell ranks seventh among wide receivers in ESPN's open score . The Titans ' two new cornerbacks,  Alontae Taylor and Cor'Dale Flott , were both below average last season in my  pre-throw cornerback positioning metric .

 
 

 

 Jordyn Brooks , LB, Miami Dolphins : 14 tackles, 1 tackle for loss, 45% run stop win rate

 Raiders coach Klint Kubiak used a run-heavy offense last season in Seattle. I have to imagine he'll want to do the same with  Kirk Cousins , 38, at quarterback and a lacking receiver group that lost  Brock Bowers  ( meniscus trim ) for Week 1. Add in that the Raiders are favored -- therefore more likely to be leading -- and that should equate to even more rushes for rookie Mike Washington Jr . and (presumably) Ashton Jeanty  ( ankle ).

 Brooks is the defender most likely to absorb those runs and convert them into tackles. Last season, he ranked fifth among linebackers in tackle rate versus run plays (25%) and 12th in run stop win rate (37%).

 

 

 Moody predicts three fantasy sleepers 
 

 Jalen Coker , WR, Carolina Panthers (rostered in 51.4% of ESPN leagues) 

 From Week 8 through Carolina's wild-card loss , Coker played 73% of the snaps and handled a 17.8% target share. He flashed his upside in the playoffs against the Rams, finishing with nine receptions for 134 yards and a touchdown.

 Coker is projected for the second-most targets on the Panthers behind Tetairoa McMillan , and both receivers have a favorable matchup against the Bears in Week 1. Chicago's defense allowed the third-most fantasy points per game to wide receivers last season.

 
 

 Malik Willis , QB, Miami Dolphins (22.1%) 

 Since 2016, there have been 23 seasons in which a quarterback started at least 16 games and averaged at least five rushing attempts per game. Those quarterbacks combined to average 21.2 fantasy points per game. Willis should easily surpass that number of attempts in Week 1, which keeps him fantasy relevant despite having one of the league's weaker supporting casts. Plus, the Raiders allowed 16.0 fantasy points per game to quarterbacks last season.

 
 

 Michael Mayer , TE, Las Vegas Raiders (7.0%) 

 Brock Bowers will miss Week 1 after undergoing a meniscus trim , which should lead to more targets for Mayer and wide receiver  Tre Tucker (29.3%). In four games without Bowers last season, Mayer averaged 6.0 targets and 10.9 fantasy points per game.

 Quarterback  Kirk Cousins has also leaned on tight ends throughout his career, and Miami allowed the fifth-most fantasy points per game to the position last season.

 

 

 

 Bowen predicts three players to score touchdowns 
 

 Jake Ferguson , TE,  Dallas Cowboys 

 Ferguson is a priority red zone target for quarterback Dak Prescott in this offense. He saw 23 red zone targets last season, with seven of his eight touchdown grabs coming on throws inside the 20-yard line. Against the Giants on Sunday night , he can get loose on play-action concepts in the red zone. Look for him to the get the ball on corner routes and seams. 

 
 

 D'Andre Swift , RB,  Chicago Bears 

 In coach Ben Johnson's zone run game , Swift should see touches in scoring position. Last season, he had nine rushing touchdowns and 10 carries inside the 5-yard line. He'll get opportunities against a Panthers' defense that allowed 19 rushing scores in 2025 (third most in the NFL). Plus, Swift can create explosive plays as a receiver in the screen game. Those can lead to the end zone, too.

 
 

 DeVonta Smith , WR,  Philadelphia Eagles 

 After  A.J. Brown  was traded to the Patriots, Smith elevated to the No. 1 role in Philly. So, the volume will be there for him versus the Commanders' defense . Plus, we should expect more West Coast passing concepts under new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion. Watch for Smith, who has 12 touchdown receptions over his past two seasons, to score on a catch-and-run target.

 

 

 Solak makes four other wild-card predictions 
 

 The Jets will snag a pick 

 For those who (understandably) wiped the 2025 Jets season from their memory: They were the first team in NFL history to fail to secure an interception over a full season. There's no level of overall team badness that explains that -- it takes truly terrible luck.

 But fear no more! The Aaron Glenn Jets should finally get their interception in Week 1 against Cam Ward . Tennessee's offense is new across the board, with changes to its offensive coordinator and two primary receivers. And the Jets should have enough of a pass rush to force some errant throws.

 
 

 

 The Dolphins will win 

 Before you tell me there's no shot, remember how confident we all were in the Rams' dominance ... and how did they look Thursday night ? Now, the Dolphins' game against the Raiders is not in Australia, but Week 1 is known for weird results.

 With Willis as one of the league's preeminent dual-threat quarterbacks (he really is as good of a runner as Jayden Daniels ), new Dolphins offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik can deploy a ton of surprising wrinkles of which the Raiders' defensive staff has no film. The absence of…

title: Three things Bears QB Caleb Williams wants to improve on
summary: Ben Johnson laid out a careful plan for Williams' offseason tweaks, and the young QB has earned high marks.
full_text:
LAKE FOREST, Ill. -- Caleb Williams has been riding this high for months.

 An eventful offseason that saw his persona grow off the field is now over. The Bears quarterback earned the cover of Madden and became the first two-time winner of GQ's Most Stylist NFL Player. His growth in training camp was measured in several ways, from his completion percentage to recognizing the checkdown, and it left his head coach feeling certain in Williams' ascent.

 "He's doing all the things that good quarterbacks do," Ben Johnson said. "So he's going the right way. I know we talk about him every session we get. Guys, he's had a really good camp and I'm really looking forward to seeing how it comes together for him 17-plus games this year."

 When the Bears open the 2026 season at  Carolina  on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, Fox), Williams and Panthers quarterback Bryce Young will meet for the first time as starters. The 2023 trade that sent the No. 1 pick from Chicago to Carolina allowed the Panthers to draft Young and for the Bears to net five players in return over three seasons, including Williams, who was the first pick in the 2024 draft.

 Both teams have already seen a return on those investments. Williams and Young led their teams to division titles in 2025 and saw their seasons end to the same opponent: the Los Angeles Rams .

 For all the euphoric moments Williams experienced in his second season, the one that happened 239 days before Year 3 begins in earnest still haunts him.

 After forcing overtime against Los Angeles in the divisional round, Williams' pass intended for former Bears wide receiver DJ Moore was picked off and put the Rams in position to win the game with a field goal.

 "It burns," Williams said. "It's frustrating. Still. It still bothers me today, every single time the play pops up, or the Cole Kmet play pops up, it feels like it was for nothing in that sense.

 "And then you change your lens and you figure out it was meant to be."

 Eight months have passed between that game and Week 1, giving Williams and his coaches time to work through how to perform better in 2026. Here's a look at three items on Williams' offseason checklist and where he's focused on improving most.

 

 Ball placement and accuracy 
 

 Williams had the lowest completion percentage (58.1%) among qualified quarterbacks last season. That didn't stop the Bears from surging from last in total offense in 2024 to sixth in 2025 while Williams also set the franchise's single-season passing record (3,942 yards). But Johnson still wants to see the quarterback complete 70% of his throws.

 Last season, only one quarterback reached that threshold:  New England 's Drake Maye (72%). Three others who were within a percent --  San Francisco 's Mac Jones (69.6%) and Brock Purdy (69.4%) and  Buffalo 's Josh Allen (69.3%) -- were on teams that won playoff games.

 Dating to spring workouts, every pass thrown by Williams and other Bears quarterbacks was charted and gone over in the meeting room with every circumstance accounted for: dropped passes, timing of throws, where passes are placed to allow run after the catch opportunities, what the scramble drill looked like.

 That gave Williams a road map for improvement. By the middle of August, Johnson declared that Williams' accuracy was "trending upwards."

 "He's taken a lot of pride in where he's putting the ball throughout practice," Johnson said. "You see it early on in our warmup periods to routes on air, and it's translating over to the team periods as well. And yet, he still hasn't lost that stinger of being aggressive and trying to push the limits a little bit."

 The Bears generated the second-most explosive plays (127) during the 2025 regular season. Doing his part to create those gains in the passing game has made Williams stress perfection with his ball placement.

 "I think it does translate when you get on the field and there's a defense on the other side and you've had so many reps with these certain routes and these certain receivers that you get out there and execute," Williams said. "I think it does show up. Kind of the appreciation of it, talking about having the special guys that I have, really talented when running routes but also really talented when the ball's in the air. Being able to focus on those things and routes on air, giving them a good ball and then when we get out there on the field, it becomes explosive plays after that."

 

 Taking more chances 
 

 Williams has thrown 47 touchdowns and just 13 interceptions over his NFL career. He prides himself on putting the ball in places that gives his receivers the best chance at completing the catch, often erring on the side of caution.

 "That's typically how I did it for the past two years and now this year, it's a little bit more putting the ball in danger, more trust in them," Williams said. "Obviously still trying to deliver the ball, put the ball in the perfect spot for them in those moments, but it's putting the ball in a little bit more traffic, seeing the coverage, recognizing, delivering a good ball. It's trust from the plays; it's trust from the players and where they'll be and just knowing where they'll be and trusting that they'll be there."

 Williams routinely tested that throughout camp, working with receivers on scramble-drill rules to ensure they knew where to break when he extended plays. It turned unstructured secondary breaks into high-percentage completions, which were regularly seen at the end of practices in the two-minute drill.

 "Just as far as slinging it, he's doing his thing," cornerback Jaylon Johnson said. "You can see the accuracy. You can see the confidence throwing the ball in tight windows is something that's stood out to me. I just feel like top to bottom, they're a confident group."

 

 Coverage recognition 
 

 Another reason behind Williams' low number of interceptions is his familiarity, not only with the offensive scheme but how to diagnose defensive coverages more efficiently.

 Processing faster is the result of thousands of reps. Bears quarterbacks coach J.T. Barrett calls it "accelerating my vision," which allows for Williams to move off reads faster to deliver the ball on time.

 "At times you have five guys going out in a concept and so portions of the concepts are specific for certain coverages or certain looks," Williams said, "not necessarily going 1-2-3-4-5, it's, OK, we can we can skip this route because of this coverage or this post high or this split field."

 Ben Johnson challenged Williams to improve his coverage recognition over training camp. As plays got more detailed during Chicago's lengthy install, Williams' responsibility for what happens post-snap was emphasized more than last season.

 That in turn has made Williams a better student, where his preparation in the meeting room has carried out onto the practice field.

 "I write the same, like [if] it's a common concept that everybody runs in the NFL, and I write it down consistently," Williams said. "I write down what we like versus what we don't like it versus every time that the play is put in and installed. And so it's just I'm getting constant mental reps of when I see a coverage or when I see this, it's, OK, we don't like it versus this, now let's get onto the backside of the concept or another route that we that we do like in that concept."

title: Who are the winningest NFL coaches of all time?
summary: From Belichick to Reid, there are many iconic coaches in NFL history. Who has the best career record? Check out the stat breakdown now.
full_text:
Only four head coaches in NFL history have won 300 career games across the regular season and postseason. Kansas City Chiefs  coach Andy Reid was the last to cross the 300-win plateau.

 Reid recorded his 300th career victory on Jan. 18, 2025, when his Chiefs defeated the Houston Texans 23-14 in the AFC divisional round.

 Reid, who signed a five-year, $100 million extension with the Chiefs in April 2024, entered the 2026 season looking to add to his career win total and close the gap between him and the NFL's all-time winningest head coach, Hall of Famer Don Shula.

 Let's take a look at which head coaches have the most career victories in NFL history (including both regular-season and postseason play):

 *Active NFL head coach 

 5. Tom Landry, 270 wins 

 Landry was the Dallas Cowboys' head coach for an NFL-record 29 years in a row and the team had 20 consecutive winning seasons, which is also a league record. Landry led Dallas to two Super Bowl wins, defeating the Miami Dolphins in Super Bowl VI and the Denver Broncos in Super Bowl XII. He was named the NFL's Coach of the Year in 1966 and the UPI NFL Coach of the Year in 1975. Landry was an innovator, with the 4-3 defense among his creations. He was named to the NFL's 100th Anniversary All-Time Team.

 *4. Andy Reid, 307 wins 

 Reid is the only head coach in NFL history who has won 100 games with two franchises: the Philadelphia Eagles (coaching the team from 1999 through 2012) and the Chiefs (he has coached Kansas City since 2013). He led the Eagles on multiple deep playoff runs, including a Super Bowl in 2004 and three straight conference finals from 2001 to 2003. However, he wasn't able to hoist the Lombardi Trophy until he arrived in Kansas City. He has turned the Chiefs into a juggernaut, winning three Super Bowls. Reid is an offensive mastermind and quarterback whisperer. He'll likely continue to rack up wins moving forward with Patrick Mahomes , Travis Kelce & Co.

 

 3. George Halas, 324 wins 

 Halas was a co-founder of the NFL and creator of the Bears. For 10 years, he served as player-coach-executive for the Bears (which is how he earned the nickname "Mr. Everything"). In 1930, he retired as a player and focused on ownership, but he would later return to coach the Bears several times. Halas led the Bears to eight NFL championships, tying Belichick's number of titles. Halas coached the team for 40 years and had just six losing seasons. He helped create the T-formation system and used it to set an NFL record for the biggest blowout in league history: a 73-0 win over the Washington team in the 1940 NFL Championship Game. Halas was selected as the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 1963 and 1965, and he was named to the NFL's 100th Anniversary All-Time Team.

 2. Bill Belichick, 333 wins 

 Belichick is considered by some as the greatest coach in all of professional sports, as he has won an NFL-record eight Super Bowls (six as a head coach with the Patriots and two as an assistant coach with the Giants). He also ranks first among all NFL coaches in playoff wins with 31. Belichick was named the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 2003, 2007 and 2010. Many franchises have hired away Belichick's assistants and tried to replicate his "Patriot Way," but it hasn't been the same without him. If Belichick returns to NFL coaching, he is just 26 regular-season wins from surpassing Don Shula as the winningest regular-season coach of all time. 

 1. Don Shula, 347 wins 

 After playing in the NFL as a defensive back for seven seasons, Shula decided to retire and become a coach. He got his first head-coaching opportunity in 1963 with the Baltimore Colts, whom he led to the NFL championship in 1968. From 1970 through 1995, Shula had a legendary run as head coach of the Dolphins. Shula led the Dolphins to a pair of Super Bowl victories (in Super Bowl VII and Super Bowl VIII). Miami had a perfect season in 1972, making Shula the only coach in NFL history to go undefeated. He was named the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 1964, 1967, 1968 and 1972. Whether you're just counting regular-season wins (328) or including playoff wins (347), Shula is the winningest coach in NFL history.

title: Can Denver Broncos' pass rush lead the NFL in sacks in 2026?
summary: All eyes are on the Broncos' pass rush, which set single-season franchise sack records in back-to-back years -- including a league-leading 68 last season.
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- After the Denver Broncos  led the NFL in sacks with 68 last season, expectations are high for the defense entering 2026.

 "People look at us and say, 'Can they do that again?'" Broncos defensive tackle Zach Allen said. "Like, it's got to end, stats don't just repeat, there's like a regression. But we don't look at it like that. We see sacks come from playing good defense. We don't chase them; we try to earn them."

 The Broncos open the season Monday night against the Kansas City Chiefs in Arrowhead Stadium ( 8:15 p.m. ET, ABC/ESPN ) by facing Patrick Mahomes , who will be playing his first game since he tore his left ACL last December. And Denver's quest for a second straight division title begins with the league's most productive pass rush mostly intact.

 There are some slight changes. Defensive tackle John Franklin-Myers departed in free agency and edge rusher Jonathon Cooper opens the season on the commissioner's exempt list after two offseason arrests related to alleged domestic violence. But all of Denver's All-Pro selections over the past two seasons -- in which the Broncos had single-season franchise records both years -- are still in lineup. That includes Allen, edge rusher Nik Bonitto and cornerback Pat Surtain II .

 

 So, the Broncos know their slate of opponents will spend a lot of time devising a way to prevent Denver from setting another franchise high-water mark and/or pacing the league. And the defense will have to be ready to adjust in how it goes about stressing quarterbacks.

 "It's a great unit, they're motivated, they're not satisfied," Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph said. "... Our talks in meetings are always about it might not look like it did last year as far as all the numbers, that it can be different with what we're ranked -- that's not important to us. But it's about our play style, it's about being a good defense every down."

 The Broncos' pass rush is on a historic run, with 63 sacks in 2024 before the 68 last season. Those 131 sacks are the most in back-to-back seasons since the Chicago Bears had the same number spanning 1986 and 1987. The Broncos held opponents without an offensive touchdown in a league-leading five games last season and had 17 players have at least a half-sack, breaking a franchise record they tied the year before.

 "We know what we've done, but that's in the past," Broncos edge rusher Jonah Elliss said. "... We're working on being better this year."

 Elliss will be one player expected to step up as the Broncos adjust for Cooper's absence. Cooper, who was second on the team with eight sacks last season, faces a November trial on domestic violence charges and is not allowed to practice or play in games while on the commissioner's exempt list. The Broncos have mostly used Elliss and Que Robinson (a fourth-round pick in the 2025 draft) in Cooper's edge spot opposite Bonitto. Robinson had one of the team's two sacks in the preseason and led the team with three pressures.

 "All these guys we feel like can play," Broncos general manager George Paton said. "... We feel really good about [Robinson]. Then Jonah and obviously [ Dondrea Tillman ] and Nik."

 The Broncos' pass rushers believe that the cavalcade of quarterbacks they're scheduled to face this season -- a group includes Matthew Stafford , Trevor Lawrence , Justin Herbert , Brock Purdy , Aaron Rodgers , Josh Allen and Drake Maye along with Mahomes -- might be more inclined to throw quicker and attack more on first down to avoid third-and-long trouble.

 

 Or, as Joseph put it: "They know they can't lose first down, or else our pass rush comes alive."

 The Broncos were the league's toughest defense on first down last season. According to NFL Next Gen stats, opposing offenses had a success rate of just 34% on first down (a successful first-down play is at least 4 yards in a standard first-and-10 situation). That set the Broncos up on later downs, as their 12 sacks on second down were third most in the league, and their 30 sacks on third down led the NFL. So, the Broncos expect opponents to be more willing to throw quicker passes on first down and move their quarterback around to create a more difficult sack target.

 "Think we just have to be ready for the ball to be gone and to affect quarterbacks in other ways," said Allen, who led the league in quarterback hits . "But battle on first down to make it hard so we get those chances to rush."

 The Chiefs get the first spin of the wheel and will likely be without left tackle Josh Simmons , who suffered a back injury in training camp. Undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson is expected to start in Simmons' place.

 "It's just winning those battles every play," Allen said. "I think we've succeeded because we don't chase stats, we don't chase sacks. We all do our assignments so we all can make plays. If we do that then sacks come, turnovers come, we get stops and we can talk about wins. And that's what matters."

title: Can Goff, new-look Lions offense set aside disappointing 2025?
summary: After tumbling from playoff contention last season, Detroit promises a team focused on the prize in 2026.
full_text:
DETROIT -- For months, Jared Goff has fielded non-stop questions concerning the  Detroit Lions ' disappointing 2025 season.

 The veteran quarterback and his teammates will finally have a chance to put the past to rest, which Goff feels is fueling them collectively as they enter Week 1.

 "Yeah, I think so. I think it adds a little bit of a chip on your shoulder, but I think we're pretty internally motivated and want to win a championship and want to be the last team standing," Goff said. "And I think last year is a bad taste, but we've got however many chances in front of us now to go make a right."

 

 Goff and the Lions will open the 2026 season with a home contest against the New Orleans Saints on Sunday. Both teams missed the playoffs last season, have a lot to prove, and have plenty of new faces on their rosters, which adds another level of uncertainty to this early matchup.

 In a symbolic gesture, Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams  chopped his dreadlocks off on Wednesday night in anticipation of the new season, ringing in the new campaign with a new hairstyle.

 "I think it's been behind us since last season. We talked about it and we've been off of it since last year. We've been on to bigger and better things," said Williams, who is coming off back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons. "Focusing more on this year and what we've got coming up this week. New Orleans is coming in and we're just trying to get a win."

 Detroit is entering this year with a 40% chance to win the NFC North, according to ESPN Analytics, which is the highest of any team in the division. The Saints finished just 6-11 in 2025.

 Still, Lions running back  Jahmyr Gibbs isn't allowing himself to buy into those early narratives.

 "It's going to be a good game. Every team can win any given Sunday. You know that so we're not going to take anybody lightly," Gibbs said. "No matter what record they had. I mean, we didn't make the playoffs either, so I mean, they probably look at it the same way. It's going to be fun. It's going to be tough fight, but we look to win every time."

 The Lions used the offseason to sharpen their weaknesses.

 Goff, for instance, worked to develop a bond with first-year offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, which gives the QB confidence the team will be better this year than last season. For his part, Petzing said he isn't afraid to hold Goff accountable either -- or vice versa.

 

 "He's doing the same to me, asking questions, making, 'Hey, we thought about this? Do we have an answer to that? Can we do this?' I think that back and forth has been fun," Petzing said of Goff. "It's part of the job that I love, but it also makes us better."

 After failing to reach the postseason for the first time since 2022, Detroit could benefit from the league's second-easiest schedule in 2026.

 After entering their Week 8 bye with a 5-2 record last season, the Lions went 4-6 over the final 10 games. From Week 6 onward, Detroit did not win consecutive games the rest of the way.

 Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson  said nothing about last year will be carried into the upcoming season.

 "I've never been like a big chip guy. I'm more just, man, like, I don't dwell on the past too much," Hutchinson said. "I see the potential that we have, and we've had that for a few years now. So, whatever's happened in the past is forgotten and we're just going to focus everything we have on this year."

title: Career reboots: Vikings' Murray faces Packers' Gannon
summary: Jonathan Gannon coached Kyler Murray with the Cardinals, and now they seek second chances with new teams.
full_text:
The beauty of the NFL's opening weekend is the unknown. 

 With no tape to study of previous games, the Green Bay Packers will have to guess how the Minnesota Vikings might deploy new quarterback Kyler Murray on Sunday at U.S. Bank Stadium ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ). The Vikings, in turn, can only project how new Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon will scheme to stop them. 

 That Murray played for Gannon from 2023 to 2025, when Gannon was head coach of the  Arizona Cardinals , is mere coincidence in what might be the determinative schematic battle of the game. 

 "I'd say he knows exactly, probably, what [Murray] likes and doesn't like," Packers coach Matt LaFleur said of Gannon. "But it's a different scheme, a different system. There's 10 other guys out there, and I think that's a pretty good supporting cast he's got around him. There's a lot of playmakers out there. I think their O-line is one of the better O-lines in the league, so they've got a lot of talent around him." 

 Sunday's game represents a fresh start for both parties. 

 

 They were a coach-QB pairing for three years, which ended after last season. Murray did not play after Week 5 because of a foot injury, and Gannon was fired after going 15-36 in his first NFL head coaching job.

 Gannon landed in Green Bay to replace defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley, who became the Miami Dolphins ' head coach. Murray signed with the Vikings after the Cardinals released him in March and won a training camp competition with J.J. McCarthy for the starting job. 

 Thursday, Murray called Gannon "one of my favorite coaches. ... Transparent. Believed in his players no matter the circumstances."

 Not long after the preseason ended and attention turned fully to the opener, LaFleur was asked how much he will rely on Gannon to prepare for Murray and the Vikings. 

 "I think J.G. is leaning on J.G. to prepare for that," LaFleur said. 

 Murray displayed his live arm and elite open-field ability during Minnesota's training camp this summer, but his most notable struggles came when facing heavy pressure. By coincidence -- or perhaps not -- those present for Packers training camp were struck by how regularly Gannon's defenders were working on their blitz packages.

 

 Gannon could have taken a year off after he was let go by the Cardinals. He had two years left on his contract and would have been paid handsomely to do nothing. Another year in Arizona and it would match the longest he's lived in one place since his first NFL coaching job with the Falcons in 2007. 

 Instead, he waited exactly 20 days to take another job. 

 "Very grateful for the opportunity," Gannon said this week. "Put all our energy and effort into maximizing it, I know that."

 Some vagabond coaches prefer to set up a home base in one place and let their family have some sense of stability in an unstable business. Not Gannon. His wife, Gina, and their three children, Rocco, Lola and Angelo, moved with him in an indication that his stay in Green Bay might be more than a one-year stint. 

 "My eighth NFL city," Gannon said as a matter of fact.

 "They're here, they're loving life," Gannon said of his family. "They're loving life. ... School's been awesome. It's been good."

 

 LaFleur loved the idea of having another head coach on his staff, something he previously had with special teams coordinator Rich Bisaccia, even if Bisaccia was only interim head coach of the Raiders for part of a season.

 LaFleur did not set out to hire Hafley 2.0 despite the success Hafley, the former Boston College head coach, had in his two seasons with the Packers before he was hired by the Dolphins. 

 "I had a pretty good idea of the man we were getting when we got him," LaFleur said of Gannon. "He understands football. He understands offensive football, which I think is imperative when you're in one of those roles -- you'd better know the other side of the ball. And he understands the importance of trying to give similar looks and have different things off of that.

 "So I think he does a great job. He's a great communicator. He holds these guys to a high standard now."

 From the players' perspective, the transition from Hafley to Gannon has been smooth. As well-liked as Hafley was, players have taken to Gannon just as quickly. Player after player has raved about Gannon's energy, innovation and scheme. 

 No one seems to care about the lack of success by Gannon in Arizona. 

 "I see why they [brought] him in here," Packers cornerback Keisean Nixon said. 

 If one thing has stood about Gannon so far, it's his willingness to adjust. 

 

 His defenses in Arizona, run by coordinator Nick Rallis, did not feature much blitzing. In fact, the Cardinals had the lowest blitz rate in the league among the 32 teams during Gannon's first season (2023) and then ranked 17th and 19th in blitz rate the following two seasons. When Gannon was the coordinator with the Philadelphia Eagles , his defenses ranked 30th and 22nd in blitz rate. 

 Yet the most noticeable thing about Gannon's defense this summer in training camp was how often -- and with so many different players -- that he blitzed. Gannon blitzed linebackers Edgerrin Cooper and Zaire Franklin up the middle, brought cornerbacks off the edge and safeties from the slot.

 Murray's struggles against the Vikings' blitz packages in camp are relevant and reflect his performance against it in recent seasons. Looking at a recent sample size, beginning with the 2024 season, Murray's QBR against the blitz (65) is slightly below the NFL average (69). 

 

 In Minnesota this summer, public attention focused more on McCarthy's fate and future than it did on Murray, the 2019 No. 1 draft pick, who is seeking a career restart at age 29. As the page turns to the regular season, with McCarthy now positioned as the No. 3 quarterback, Murray will take center stage.

 He begins with a clean slate after seven years of mixed reviews with the Cardinals, as the Vikings' veteran roster absorbed him in ways that a less-established group might not have. Known in Arizona as an introvert, Murray has found ways to connect -- and direct -- players from receiver Justin Jefferson to running back Aaron Jones Sr .

 "He has a different way of leading," Jones said. "He'll come and wrap his arms around you on the side. Give you some words, get on the same page, different things like that. It might not be to everybody [at once], but he's making sure he's getting his words in to each and everybody, one by one. You get a little more of a personal relationship like that."

 Murray told ESPN earlier this month that he hoped to make 2026 his " best season ever " and could not stop smiling this week when asked about Sunday's matchup.

 "I don't know how many years I played football," he said Thursday, "[but] this has got to be right up there for most anticipated. I can't tell you how excited and ready I am just to be on the field again."

 Gannon kept his comments vanilla when asked about Murray early in the week.

 "Really good player," Gannon said of his former quarterback. "He's in a really good offense with some elite players. Obviously I've got nothing but love and respect for K1. He's competitive, he's smart, can make all the throws, and beat you with his legs. So big time challenge."

 As this week went on and the final touches were being placed on the game plan, Packers players could tell this was a different kind of week because of their coordinator's connection to the opposing quarterback. They left little doubt that Gannon has given them some extra notes on Murray.

 "He gives a lot of respect to that quarterback, I'll say that much, as he should," Packers safety Evan Williams said. "He's done some great things in this league. He does a lot with his feet, is able to extend plays, is able to make plays on the run.

 "A guy like that isn't a first overall pick for nothing. So a lot of respect for him, but JG got answers. He's always got…

title: Which Jaguars WRs will lead in catches, TDs, yards in 2026?
summary: Brian Thomas Jr., Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers will compete for Trevor Lawrence's targets when the season starts Sunday vs. the Browns.
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Wide receiver  Parker Washington  had a breakout season in 2025 and led the Jacksonville Jaguars in receptions, receiving yards and receiving touchdowns. Fellow receiver  Brian Thomas Jr . led all three categories as a rookie in 2024. But if things go the way head coach Liam Coen envisions, there could be three different names atop each of those categories in 2026.

 The plan is to have quarterback Trevor Lawrence  spread the ball around because the offense is more effective when the passing game isn't focused on one receiver -- and it makes it harder for defenses to stop. 

 "It's obviously sometimes a good problem to have," Coen said. "These guys know that every one of them is going to have plays schemed for them. There's no question. All those guys will have that, and then it's just within the play, within the progressions, within the alerts, they're going to have to eat, as well. ... And I think that's the good thing about the group all being talented and having their own roles is within any given play, especially the way Trevor scrambles, every eligible is alive."

 Washington, Thomas and Jakobi Meyers are the Jaguars' top three receivers in 2026, and each brings something a little different to the offense, a versatility Meyers said is the group's strength.

 "Balance," he said. "That's the best way to describe us, honestly. I think we've got a very well-balanced room. ... We've got guys who are smart, first and foremost, [and] who understand what they're doing. And then second, can make a bunch of plays. So, I think we're in a good spot."

 Thomas, with his 4.33 speed, stretches the field and can be a deep-ball threat. He struggled with drops and injuries in 2025 but had an encouraging offseason.

 "When you can throw the ball over somebody's head, it's a threat," Coen said. "And it's something that we need."

 

 The Jaguars traded for Meyers on Nov. 4, and he instantly helped spark an offense that was averaging 20.4 points, 212.3 passing yards and 321.1 total yards per game. The Jaguars' numbers increased to 31.3 points, 228.6 passing yards and 336 total yards per game after his arrival. There was instant trust between Meyers and Lawrence, who described Meyers as an "easy guy to throw to" because Meyers made what he was going to do with his route clear. Of Meyers' 42 catches, more than half (28) went for first downs -- the most of anyone on the team in that nine-game span.

 "I hate to use the word reliable [because] I feel like it almost kind of knocks him down a peg, which is not the case," Coen said. "It's just you know he's going to do right. You know he's going to, the majority of the time, get open. He's so quarterback-friendly in that he understands concepts, I think, differently than most receivers."

 Washington is a threat on all three levels and is good after the catch; a team-high 32.5% of his 847 receiving yards last season came after the catch. Washington averaged 14.6 yards per catch last season, but that number was a team-high 16.7 once Meyers joined the team.  

 There is also 2025 No. 2 pick  Travis Hunter , who will be a starting cornerback but also a receiver on offense on select plays. The receivers are embracing the plan for a mix and look at it as a positive, even though that might mean sacrificing some stats at times.

 "That makes this offense unique, and we've just been trying to fine-tune and really hone in on what each guy is great at," Washington said.

 In his annual projections , ESPN senior fantasy football writer Mike Clay predicted the Jaguars' leaders in catches, yards and touchdowns. Using those and what I've seen during the preseason, let's look at what to expect ahead of the season kicking off Sunday against the Cleveland Browns at EverBank Stadium (1 p.m. ET).

 

 Catches 
 Clay's projection: 
1. Meyers (70) 
2. Washington (64) 
3. Thomas (57) 
4. Hunter (38)

 My take : This one isn't super surprising because Meyers was the Jaguars' leading receiver in 2025. He caught 42 passes on 61 targets in nine games. Washington was second in both categories (33 catches on 52 targets), though he missed one game because of a hip injury.

 

 However, by the end of the season, Washington had emerged as Lawrence's top target. In the final four games (including the playoff loss to Buffalo), Washington led the Jaguars in targets (42), receptions (26), receiving yards (454), average per catch (17.5) and touchdown catches (three). No other player had more than 16 catches (Meyers) or 140 yards receiving (Meyers) in that stretch.

 Washington was the offense's most impressive player in training camp, so he will challenge Meyers for the team lead.

 
 Receiving yards 
 Clay's projection: 
1. Thomas (860) 
2. Washington (852) 
3. Meyers (766) 
4. Hunter (449)

 My take: This offseason, Thomas worked on his hands, got stronger at the catch point and is in a much better headspace. Coen made it a priority for Lawrence and Thomas to work on stretching the field with deeper throws, and they showed in the spring that they had developed better chemistry with that.

 If the Jaguars can push the ball down the field more with Thomas, things should open on the intermediate and shorter levels for Washington and Meyers. Washington's run-after-catch ability and toughness as a runner -- he had 158 receiving yards after first contact last season, and no one else on the Jaguars had more than 34 -- will help him pile up yards and compete for the lead in the category. Coen wanting the ball spread around more should keep the three receivers in the same range yardage-wise.

 
 Receiving touchdowns 
 Clay's projection: 
1. Meyers, Washington and Thomas (5) 
4. Hunter (3)

 My take: It's a tie! This is the hardest one to predict. The Jaguars added two tight ends in the draft --  Nate Boerkircher and Tanner Koziol -- and both are big red zone targets for Lawrence. Coen wants to use more 12 personnel with Brenton Strange and Boerkircher, and that should open more receiving opportunities for Strange.

 Then there's the Hunter factor: He will be primarily a cornerback, but he will have a role on offense, and the Jaguars rotated him and Thomas on the field during camp when using three-receiver sets. Thomas looked so good in the spring and in training camp, and Coen said throwing the ball down the field is a priority in 2026. That should mean more production from Thomas, especially in TD catches.

title: Why Mike McDaniel and Jim Harbaugh 'need each other' this season in L.A.
summary: We talked to Chargers OC Mike McDaniel and coach Jim Harbaugh about their football marriage.
full_text:
MIKE MCDANIEL RAN toward  Jim Harbaugh, yelling, "You feel the juice, coach?"

 It was the first day of the  Los Angeles Chargers ' 2026 training camp. The beginning of a new partnership for these coaches. And Harbaugh was, in fact, feeling the juice.

 "I'm trying to curb my enthusiasm," Harbaugh said.

 "Good luck ... People can't even help themselves," replied McDaniel.

 "I think of it like all of the investment that's been made. I had a coach who used to say, 'It's like putting money in the bank, now it's time to start withdrawing, taking some dividends, right?'" Harbaugh said.

 

 "I've never wanted training camp to start more," McDaniel said as the two locked eyes, him wearing gray jogger capris that stopped just below his knees and bright blue designer Air Forces; Harbaugh wearing his team-issued Chargers polo, trousers, sneakers and hat.

 A match made in football heaven -- or something like that.

 McDaniel, the Chargers' new offensive coordinator, and Harbaugh, the team's coach of three seasons, arrived at this partnership from vastly different circumstances. Once one of the league's most promising head coaches, known for his offensive prowess, McDaniel was fired after four seasons with the Miami Dolphins and criticized for lacking the authority to be a coach.

 Harbaugh is a commanding veteran leader known for quickly turning middling teams into winners, but in two seasons in L.A., mediocre offenses have kept this team from advancing in the playoffs.

 That dichotomy brought Harbaugh, 62, and McDaniel, 43, together this offseason. "He reminds me of a young Jimmy Harbaugh ... sometimes it's like looking in the mirror," Harbaugh said, before clarifying that he never dressed like McDaniel.

 Despite their fashion differences, they share a football philosophy centered on winning at the line of scrimmage and running the football. More importantly, each offers what the other needs at this stage in their careers.

 Harbaugh needs McDaniel to jump-start an offense that has kept his teams from contending, while McDaniel needs to absorb elements of Harbaugh's leadership style if he hopes to become an improved head coach again. Their football marriage is central to the Chargers' title hopes, a quest that begins in earnest Week 1 when the Bolts host the Arizona Cardinals at SoFi Stadium ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 "We need each other," McDaniel told ESPN of his partnership with Harbaugh. "But that's kind of the beauty of the National Football League ... you learn quickly that every year you are putting your career in the hands of all of your teammates."

 
 

 MCDANIEL YELLS A LOT. Despite often being one of the smallest people at Chargers practice at 5-foot-9, he's one of the loudest -- frequently reminding the defense that they can't stop his plays or pumping up a player.

 One day, weeks into training camp, he was running around the practice field yelling, "F--- yeah, 10." Moments before, quarterback Justin Herbert threw a pass up and over the arms of safety  RJ Mickens  and into the hands of tight end David Njoku for a roughly 40-yard completion. It was an impressive completion, but on the surface, it was the kind of throw to be expected of Herbert.

 For McDaniel, it represented more. It was the latest example of his star quarterback executing a challenge in an offseason that has been about relearning how Herbert plays the position. On this play, McDaniel asked Herbert to read the post safety, Mickens, early in his drop and throw the ball with anticipation. Herbert had previously been waiting too long for McDaniel's liking or throwing with a slight hitch.

 "It was the first time that he had kind of recognized and been able to do the read super fast like we've been talking about," McDaniel said. "Those types of things [are] becoming a regular occurrence. Every practice, there's something new that we're working on that he's trying to get done."

 For the past two seasons, the formula for the back-to-back 11-win Chargers has been straightforward: Rely on an elite, Jesse Minter-led defense that holds opponents to below 20 points per game, then hope Herbert makes a few hero plays per game to keep the offense afloat.

 

 Each season, that recipe fell apart in the playoffs. Over two playoff games under former offensive coordinator Greg Roman, the Chargers scored just one touchdown, featuring two of the worst performances that Herbert had as a pro.

 After the Chargers' 16-3 wild-card loss to the New England Patriots in January, Harbaugh fired Roman, the only offensive coordinator he had in the NFL. Together, they had reached three conference championship games and a Super Bowl when he and Harbaugh held the same roles with the San Francisco 49ers from 2011 to 2014.

 Poor injury luck contributed to Roman's offensive struggles. But beyond that, he struggled to consistently scheme receivers open and ran an offense that lacked innovation as defenses evolved.

 In many ways, McDaniel is the antithesis of Roman. Known for his innovative motions and condensed formations that put opposing defenses in a bind, McDaniel's offensive approach has changed offenses across the league. Former Buffalo Bills coach Sean McDermott called McDaniel's offense in Miami "revolutionary." San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan admitted he stole some of McDaniel's pre-snap motions in 2023.

 "Really been doing a lot of listening, a lot of learning, a lot of leaning into how he sees football because it's really brilliant," Harbaugh said of his new OC.

 Since he took the job in January, McDaniel has been focused on helping Herbert "own" the position. He has changed Herbert's shotgun stance, moved his nonthrowing side foot forward (in other words, his left foot in front of his right) and has emphasized anticipatory throwing.

 Shortly after he got the job, McDaniel watched every snap Herbert has taken in the NFL. McDaniel then put together a video featuring hundreds of plays from Herbert's career and juxtaposed them with similar plays from McDaniel's previous offenses to prove that if Herbert made the adjustments McDaniel was coaching him to make, he could be more successful.

 "It was a well-put-together presentation, and I really saw the vision," Herbert said. "It meant a lot to me."

 The detailed coaching goes beyond Herbert. McDaniel's wide zone rushing scheme has the offensive line running more than it ever has in practice. Offensive line coach Butch Barry's screams are among the few to rival McDaniel's yells at practice.

 Barry's commands are so loud they can likely be heard throughout L.A., as he yells at Chargers linemen to run faster. It's been an adjustment for the pass catchers, too. "That ball's coming out fast," tight end Scott Matlock said during one minicamp practice. The emphasis on anticipatory throwing has altered how receivers are coached to run their routes, with McDaniel imploring them to look back for the ball earlier than they've been asked to before.

 In doing so, they'll get the ball earlier in their break with more opportunity for yards after the catch.

 "You think that the ball's quick and then you get Mike's offense and there's a whole different element," wide receiver Ladd McConkey said.

 McDaniel's offensive plan is all about making life easy for Herbert, the opposite of what it's been in the Harbaugh era so far.

 But McDaniel's style comes with its flaws, too, all of which led him to Harbaugh and L.A.

 
 

 TWO DECADES AGO, McDaniel was first introduced to who Harbaugh is.

 McDaniel played wide receiver at Yale University from 2001 to 2004. During his sophomore year, Yale blew out the University of San Diego 49-14, a team that, to McDaniel, seemed far away from being of the same caliber.

 But just two years after McDaniel graduated, the paradigm had shifted. San Diego had a new coach -- Jim Harbaugh -- and they dominated his alma mater Yale, beating them 43-14 in 2006, in their second straight win against the Ivy.

 Harbaugh never coached…

title: Fred Warner jabs at Rams on social media after 49ers win
summary: The 49ers linebacker didn't hold back on social media after the team's Melbourne win.
full_text:
After the San Francisco 49ers  pounded the Los Angeles Rams in Melbourne, linebacker  Fred Warner didn't hold back his thoughts on social media.

 

 The Niners delivered a 27-7 loss to the Rams on Thursday night, with the defense allowing just a second-quarter touchdown to Rams running back Kyren Williams .

 After Los Angeles scored that touchdown, the Rams performed a sleep celebration in the end zone, a possible reference to talk about the different travel approaches the teams took ahead of their Week 1 matchup, with the 49ers leaving a little more than a week before the game while the Rams arrived the day before it.

 Warner held on to the receipts.

 After his performance, in which he led San Francisco with 11 total tackles, Warner posted a carousel of photos to Instagram with the caption "Google Me."

 While the first few photos showed Warner in action, the last three slides quickly turned into trolls of the Rams.

 

 Warner used a video of Daejon Love, a 35-year-old man who was arrested on fraud charges  after posing as a 49ers and Rams player.

 In the video, Love says he's "about to play with the Rams" while wearing Los Angeles gear.

 Love was arrested by the FBI on Aug. 24 with accomplice Taylor Jamie Chan after defrauding around two dozen women out of $1.3 million.

 But Warner didn't stop there.

 He included a snippet of Rams head coach Sean McVay's comments about their travels to Melbourne.

 "Flight was great, we feel well rested," McVay said in the clip.

 To put the icing on the cake, Warner capped the carousel with the Rams' sleep celebration.

 If anyone got the last laugh, it was certainly Warner.

title: Betting buzz: Rams suffer worst opening loss by preseason Super Bowl favorite in 50 years
summary: The Los Angeles Rams' defeat in Week 1 in Melbourne, Australia was a historic low for a preseason Super Bowl champion.
full_text:
Everything that happens in sports has additional context when viewed from a sports betting perspective. From season-changing injuries to record-setting moments and so much more, the sports news cycle will constantly and significantly affect the sports betting industry. 

 Our NFL betting buzz file, with contributions from David Purdum, Doug Greenberg and others, aims to provide fans a look at the sports betting stories that are driving the conversation throughout each week of the season.  

 Key links: NFL futures | Awards odds |  Sports betting home  |  DraftKings   

 

 Sept 11: Rams suffer worst opening loss by preseason Super Bowl favorite in 50 years 

 by David Purdum 

 Preseason Super Bowl favorites have lost before, just not as badly as the Los Angeles Rams did Thursday in Melbourne, Australia.

 The Rams lost 27-7 to the San Francisco 49ers , becoming the first preseason Super Bowl favorite to lose its opener by 20 or more in the past 50 seasons, according to SportsOddHistory.com. The 1993 Dallas Cowboys lost by 19, and the 2017 New England Patriots and 1987 New York Giants each lost by 15 in their season openers. Both the Cowboys and Patriots would play in the Super Bowl in those seasons, with the Cowboys winning and the Patriots losing, but the Giants failed to make the playoffs.

 Los Angeles closed as a 3.5-point favorite over the 49ers and attracted the bulk of the bets and money from bettors. BetMGM reported that 60% of the money bet on the point spread was on the Rams.

 The Rams have attracted more than twice as many bets to win the Super Bowl as any other team at DraftKings Sportsbook. They remain the favorites to win the Super Bowl, NFC and NFC West, but their odds dipped from 5-1 to 6-1 after Thursday's loss, and their odds to win the NFC West shifted from -105 to +164.

 The 49ers, in turn, improved from +300 to +180 to win the division. The defending-champion Seattle Seahawks moved from +215 to +184 in the tightly contested NFC West. San Francisco improved from 19-1 to 14-1 to win the Super Bowl at DraftKings.

title: How Raiders' QB Kirk Cousins is approaching Year 15
summary: We spoke to Raiders' Kirk Cousins about the 2026 season, working with Klint Kubiak and his role as a mentor.
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- Kirk Cousins will begin his 15th season in the NFL on Sunday against the Miami Dolphins . And for the Las Vegas Raiders quarterback, that milestone has a ton of meaning.

 It's a sign of his resilience throughout his NFL journey. When Cousins was drafted by Washington  in 2012, serving as a backup behind former quarterback Robert Griffin III, he didn't have any idea that his career would reach this point. Eventually, he emerged as a full-time starter for his final three seasons in Washington before playing six seasons as the starter for the Minnesota Vikings .

 "I remember going out to minicamp my rookie year [in Washington] and just being grateful that I got to wear an NFL helmet for one practice," Cousins told ESPN. "I always felt like I was one year at a time, one day at a time sometimes, and taking that one day at a time mentality has led me here."

 

 Year 15 also represents the generational gap between him and his new teammates in Las Vegas. As a member of the Raiders, Cousins' third team in four seasons, he is the oldest player on the roster at 38. He is one of three players who are at least 30, with left tackle Kolton Miller being the second-oldest at 31.

 If Maxx Crosby , 29, puts himself in unc status among his teammates -- the average roster age for Las Vegas is 26 -- he said Cousins is a tier above.

 "He's headed towards senior [citizen]. Nah, I'm just playing," Crosby said jokingly. "He's the oldest of the group, for sure. But he brings great energy, too. That's one thing I give him a lot of credit for. He never shies away from cracking jokes and being one of the guys, and he's been incredible."

 Cousins being the elder of the team has come with benefits. It has led to frequent jokes between him and the other players. During the spring, Cousins asked players if they had seen the 1995 film "Heavyweights," starring Ben Stiller, and barely anyone knew what he was talking about.

 Cousins recalled second-year right guard Caleb Rogers bringing up the 1984 movie "Red Dawn," asking if he had seen it.

 "[Rogers] said, 'Yeah, I figured you had seen it because I knew it was from your era,'" Cousins said. "And then I looked up to see it was from 1984, and I was like, 'Well, I wasn't born until '88, but I understand what you're saying."

 His presence is also essential for the Raiders, who are in the midst of a rebuild, and his familiarity with new coach Klint Kubiak's scheme can help get the young talent, including No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza , up to speed. That's why he is fit to begin the season, which starts Sunday at home against the Miami Dolphins ( 4:25 p.m. on Fox ), as the team's starting quarterback.

 "As a quarterback, you want to help the next tier guys to elevate their play," Cousins said. "I think that's what quarterbacking in this league is about; trying to help elevate the guys around you, so that when you step in the huddle, 10 guys play better, and also enjoy relating with the coaches and building a bond with them where you can finish each other's sentences."

 

 WHEN THE ATLANTA Falcons released Cousins in March, he wasn't sure where his career would go next. Sitting in limbo, Cousins wondered if Atlanta's Week 18 win over the New Orleans Saints in January 2026 would be his final NFL game ever.

 

 The past three years have been somewhat of a roller coaster for Cousins. His final season with the Vikings ended abruptly when he suffered a torn Achilles eight games into the 2023 season. The injury, however, didn't prevent Cousins from signing a four-year, $180 million contract with the Falcons in 2024.

 Soon after, Atlanta drafted Michael Penix Jr . with the eighth overall pick of the 2024 draft. Cousins started in 14 games that fall but threw a league-high 16 interceptions before he was benched. Last season, Penix suffered a torn ACL , forcing Cousins to start the last seven games. He threw for 1,471 passing yards with 10 touchdowns and five interceptions to close the season.

 Cousins was let go on the first day of the 2026 league year . And eventually, Kubiak called .

 "Before Klint called, you have to ask yourself, 'What's next if I'm done?'" Cousins said. "Then I had the opportunity to come to [Las Vegas], and you focus on the task at hand."

 

 Cousins came to Las Vegas and joined an organization that's starting from scratch after posting a 3-14 record in 2025. Despite the frequent coaching and front office turnover in recent years, Cousins said the current regime -- Kubiak, general manager John Spytek and minority owner Tom Brady -- has given him the belief that they can rebuild the team the right way.

 Cousins said the Raiders have a system in place for what's needed to win in the NFL, starting with commitment from the top down on a shared vision. Kubiak's staff features coaches who have been with him at previous stops, including offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko and offensive line coach Rick Dennison.

 Cousins even spent time in Minnesota being coached by Kubiak and his father, Gary Kubiak, who was an assistant head coach and offensive coordinator/adviser from 2019-20. That's why Cousins is important to help jump-start this rebuild. He has a firm understanding of Kubiak's expectations and how the offense should be run, and he can relay that message to the rest of the team.

 "He brings a lot of experience to the room, a lot of plays in this league," Janocko said. "... As we learn and we grow, we can feed from some of the knowledge that he brings to the table."

 

 COUSINS' PRESENCE HAS allowed some players to relive their childhood. He remembered walking past a player in the weight room who said to Cousins that he used him when playing Madden in middle school.

 Cousins has had players who are from the Maryland and D.C. area say "You like that?!" when he walks past them.

 "I'd dap them up and introduce myself, and they say, 'Man, I remember when you said that I was in seventh grade or whatever the age is, and so they date you a little bit," Cousins said.

 Cousins has had fun interacting with the younger players. Moments like when teammates reference some of his viral moments or pop culture conversations remind him of the large age gap that has made him smile. He would sometimes go home to his sons and ask them about stuff he heard at work so he could stay hip with everything.

 

 Recently, teammates made Cousins aware of the value of Pokemon cards in 2026, compared to when he was growing up.

 "There were Pokemon cards when I was in the third grade, but they weren't quite where they are now in terms of the dollar value and the collecting," he said. "So I was like, update me on where Pokemon cards are now because I knew where they were in 1997."

 Players have joked about Cousins telling dad jokes around the facility and his style, which includes cargo shorts and a T-shirt. "One of the teammates said [to Cousins], 'Hey, nice cargo shorts today.' I looked up at bro and was like, 'Yeah, he looks like a dad right now,'" second-year offensive tackle Charles Grant said.

 Truth is, Cousins has always been an old soul. In Washington, Cousins said All-Pro offensive tackle Trent Williams gave him a hard time for wearing Mall Walkers shoes. Others would tell him that he had "nerd swag" or "his swag is having no swag."

 "I guess now I've grown into the vibe that I always had," Cousins said. "I just had it in my 20s. Now I'm actually in my late 30s, and I'm a dad of two boys, and so the vibe probably fits better now. But it's really always been my shtick."

 

 Cousins has a great admiration for the Raiders' young core. Among those players are second-year running back Ashton Jeanty , Rogers, and rookies such as Mendoza, running back Mike Washington Jr . and wide receiver Malik Benson .

 He has been impressed with their work ethic and willingness to learn, and jokingly said they have improved his hope for the younger generation.

title: Dolphins rookie WRs ready for the spotlight
summary: New Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said the rookies will start the opener because they deserve it.
full_text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- There's no gamesmanship involved with the Dolphins' first depth chart of the season.

 Rookies Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell were listed as starting wide receivers ahead of Sunday's game against the Las Vegas Raiders (4:25 p.m., E.T., FOX), and coach Jeff Hafley said it's not a fluke or a formality -- the rookies have earned their spot.

 "Winning is the priority. We're not going to put a guy out there Week 1 just to see what we have," he said. "We believe those guys deserve to start, and we're going to start them. And we'll find out what we need to work on, how we need to develop them, with winning as a priority."

 Douglas has worked with the Dolphins' first team since early in training camp and started their preseason opener against the Washington Commanders ; his inclusion among Miami's Week 1 starters was no surprise.

 Dolphins wide receivers coach Tyke Tolbert said Douglas has an "it factor," although that doesn't mean there won't be rookie moments for the third-round pick.

 "He makes some plays. He has some wiggle; he has some speed," Tolbert said. "He can make plays on balls outside the frame of his body. Some of those things that we liked in the draft process and we liked in training camp, and he's been making some of those plays.

 "We wish he could catch everything and have every assignment correctly, but the fact of the matter is none of the rookies are doing that right now. But he's coming along really, really well. We really like where he is."

 Bell, on the other hand, played just 13 snaps in the preseason, all in the finale against the New York Giants . He spent most of the offseason rehabbing a torn ACL suffered in December, but was activated off the non-football injury list Aug. 17, and was cleared for full contact a week later.

 His return to the practice field was well ahead of schedule; though the team was initially coy about his rehab timeline, general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan eventually revealed the team thought he'd be ready after its Week 6 bye.

 Bell is still getting back into playing shape, although Hafley said he won't be on a snap count this week. Despite that, the third-round pick's coaches say his talent is obvious -- and impossible to ignore.

 "He's been putting the work day in and day out, and he's come along so strongly to the point where ... [we said] why wait til the bye -- he's ready," Tolbert said. "Now, again, he's behind some of those other guys. He doesn't have the banked reps those other guys have ... but he's catching on. He has a ways to go, but he's up to the point where he's so talented that you have to put him on the field and see what he can do."

 Similar to Miami, the Raiders are also one of the youngest teams in the league, but have a fairly experienced secondary. Safety Jeremy Chinn and cornerback Eric Stokes have been in the league since 2020 and 2021, respectively, while cornerback Taron Johnson is entering his ninth NFL season.

 

 Also similar to the Dolphins, Las Vegas hired a new head coach and coordinators this offseason, so there will be a fair amount of uncertainty for both sides come Sunday.

 Dolphins offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik said he'll be paying attention to how his rookie receivers respond to a hostile environment Sunday, and how they adjust to what he described as a fluid game plan.

 "Your first game's on the road; you got to deal with crowd noise," Slowik said. "Obviously, there's pretty good players on defense that you're going against. What happens during the game that creates adversity? How do you respond to that? And do you rise to the occasion, or do you sink? That's what we're going to be looking for.

 "Like, there's going to be a lot of adjustments in this game. There's going to be a lot of things; both sides are going to have to do just from not having much to go off of before we kind of get into this thing, which is why we really got to hang our hat on the style of play. And once that starts to fade -- and it happens sometimes to young guys when they get in that environment. It's our job as coaches, we got to bring them up."
